## Learning goals

Inflation is the growth rate of the overall price level. By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- measure inflation from a price index, derive average inflation and the rule of 70 from the definition, and
  convert a price from one year into the dollars of another year with the consumer price index (CPI);
- derive the **quantity theory of money** step by step from its four assumptions, and solve it for the price level,
  $P^* = \bar{M}\bar{V}/\bar{Y}$, and for inflation, $\pi^* = \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y$;
- read the **comparative statics** of the quantity theory, and explain why money is **neutral** in the long run
  (the **classical dichotomy**);
- test the quantity theory with 150 years of U.S. data and with 165 economies;
- derive the **Fisher equation**, $i = R + \pi$, from the return on one saved dollar, and use it to compute real interest
  rates and to see who gains and who loses from surprise inflation;
- derive how much revenue a government raises by printing money (**seigniorage**), and explain why very high
  inflation is usually a **fiscal** problem;
- rebuild a price index from inflation rates, compute average growth rates over periods, use ratio scales
  with clear tick labels, and spot suspicious numbers in a data set.

```{python}
#| kind: helper
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each model figure gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: helper
# @title Helpers for the website's country legends (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def legend_only(fig, keep):
    """Website: every trace not named in keep starts hidden but stays in the legend (click to show it).

    Slider steps keep the choice, so a slider never switches on all countries at once.
    """
    names = [t.name for t in fig.data]
    for t in fig.data:
        if t.visible is not False and t.name not in keep:
            t.visible = "legendonly"
    for slider in fig.layout.sliders:
        steps = []
        for step in slider.steps:
            shown = []
            for name, v in zip(names, step.args[0]["visible"]):
                shown.append(v if (v is False or name in keep) else "legendonly")
            steps.append(dict(method=step.method, label=step.label, args=[{"visible": shown}, step.args[1]]))
        slider.steps = steps
    return fig


def scale_buttons(fig, ratio_ticks, start="linear"):
    """Website: linear/ratio buttons; the vertical axis then fits whatever countries are shown."""
    linear = dict(label="linear scale", method="relayout",
                  args=[{"yaxis.type": "linear", "yaxis.autorange": True, "yaxis.tickvals": None}])
    ratio = dict(label="ratio scale", method="relayout",
                 args=[{"yaxis.type": "log", "yaxis.autorange": True, "yaxis.tickvals": ratio_ticks}])
    buttons = [linear, ratio] if start == "linear" else [ratio, linear]
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(type="buttons", direction="right", x=0.01, y=0.98, xanchor="left",
                                        yanchor="top", buttons=buttons)])
    fig.update_yaxes(autorange=True)
    return fig
```

## Model overview

Inflation is the rate at which prices rise on average. A few percent a year hardly gets noticed, but over decades it adds up, and in some countries prices have doubled every few weeks. This chapter asks what causes inflation in the long run, how it changes interest rates, and why some governments let it get out of hand. The answer it builds on is an old one: prices rise when money grows faster than the goods and services it buys.

This section works through the chapter's ideas in five blocks, each going from assumptions to results. First come the definitions we need to measure inflation. Then the **quantity theory of money** explains the price level and the inflation rate, and it shows why money is **neutral** in the long run. The **Fisher equation** links inflation to interest rates. A short block uses it to see who gains and who loses when inflation is a surprise or when taxes ignore it. The last block, the **government budget constraint**, explains why governments print money, and how much revenue the printing press can raise. At the end, `### The model in code` turns the key results into Python functions and checks each of them with numbers.

As in the rest of the book, a bar over a letter marks something taken as given from outside the model, such as $\bar{M}_t$ or $\bar{V}$. Letters without a bar are determined by the model. A $g$ with a subscript is a growth rate, $g_X \equiv \Delta X_{t+1}/X_t$, and $\pi$ is the inflation rate. In the text rates are in percent; in the algebra they are decimals (2 percent is 0.02). Throughout, we use one illustrative economy: money $\bar{M} = 100$, velocity $\bar{V} = 2$ and real GDP $\bar{Y} = 200$ in the starting year, money growth $\bar{g}_M = 5$ percent, real GDP growth $\bar{g}_Y = 3$ percent (the starting value of the slider in Fig. 4), and a real interest rate of 2 percent.

<!-- cell -->

### Measuring inflation

#### Definitions

**The price level.** $P_t$ is the price of a basket of goods in year $t$, written as an index: we pick a base year and set $P = 100$ there. The consumer price index (CPI) uses a basket that a typical household buys. The GDP deflator uses all of GDP.

**The inflation rate.** Inflation is the percentage change of the price level from one year to the next:

$$\pi_t = \frac{P_{t+1} - P_t}{P_t}. \tag{1}$$

When $\pi_t < 0$ the price level falls, which is called **deflation**.

**Nominal and real values.** A **nominal** value is measured in the dollars of its own year. A **real** value is measured in the dollars of one fixed year, so that it counts goods rather than dollars.

#### Working with the definitions

**From inflation back to the price level.** Multiply both sides of equation (1) by $P_t$ and add $P_t$:

$$\pi_t P_t = P_{t+1} - P_t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad P_{t+1} = (1 + \pi_t)P_t.$$

Applying this year after year chains the inflation rates together:

$$P_T = P_0(1 + \pi_0)(1 + \pi_1)\cdots(1 + \pi_{T-1}).$$

This is how Fig. 1 builds a price level from inflation rates. With a constant rate $\pi$ the product is a power, $P_T = P_0(1+\pi)^T$ ([Appendix C.3](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.3-exponents-and-exponential-growth)).

**Average inflation over many years.** Solve $P_T = P_0(1+\bar{\pi})^T$ for the constant rate $\bar{\pi}$ that links the first and the last price level. Divide by $P_0$, raise both sides to the power $1/T$, and subtract 1:

$$\left(\frac{P_T}{P_0}\right)^{1/T} = 1 + \bar{\pi} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar{\pi} = \left(\frac{P_T}{P_0}\right)^{1/T} - 1.$$

Fig. 3 measures the average growth of money and prices over decades with this formula. Taking logs gives a handy shortcut, $\bar{\pi} \approx (\ln P_T - \ln P_0)/T$ ([Appendix C.4](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.4-logarithms)).

**How long until prices double.** Set $P_T/P_0 = 2$ in $P_T = P_0(1+\pi)^T$ and take logs: $T\ln(1+\pi) = \ln 2$. Since $\ln 2 \approx 0.70$ and $\ln(1+\pi) \approx \pi$ for small $\pi$, the doubling time is about $70$ divided by inflation in percent: the **rule of 70** ([Appendix C.3](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.3-exponents-and-exponential-growth)). At 2 percent a year, prices double in about 35 years.

**Moving a price from one year to another.** A good that cost $X_a$ dollars in year $a$ cost the same share of the basket as $X_a \times P_b/P_a$ dollars in year $b$. The "year-$a$ dollars" cancel, like units in a conversion:

$$X_b = X_a \times \frac{P_b}{P_a}. \tag{2}$$

Only the ratio $P_b/P_a$ matters, so the choice of base year makes no difference ([Appendix C.2](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.2-percentages-ratios-and-index-numbers)). If the price level doubles from 100 to 200, a 50-dollar item of the first year is a 100-dollar item of the second.

#### What it tells us

- Small rates add up. At 2 percent a year the price level doubles in 35 years, so a dollar of today buys about half of what a dollar bought 35 years ago.
- Anything fixed in dollars loses value at the rate of inflation. A pension of 1,000 dollars a year that is never raised buys, after 35 years at 2 percent, what 500 dollars bought when it started: its real value is $1{,}000 \times P_0/P_T$.
- A price index only compares years. To say whether gasoline was cheap in some past year, convert its price into today's dollars with equation (2) before comparing it with today's price.

<!-- cell -->

### The quantity theory of money

#### Assumptions

Money is whatever people use to pay for things. Think of it first as paper currency; Table 8.2 lists broader measures that add bank deposits. Four variables enter the theory, and four equations pin them down.

**1. The quantity equation.** Each dollar is spent several times a year. The **velocity of money** $V_t$ counts how many times, on average. So $M_t$ dollars buy $M_tV_t$ dollars of goods in a year. That spending is nominal GDP, the price level times real GDP:

$$M_tV_t = P_tY_t. \tag{3}$$

On its own, equation (3) is close to a definition: given $M$, $P$ and $Y$, it measures velocity, $V = PY/M$. In our economy nominal GDP is $1 \times 200 = 200$ and money is 100, so each dollar changes hands twice a year. It becomes a theory once we add three more equations.

**2. The classical dichotomy.** Real GDP is set by real forces only: capital, labor, ideas and productivity, as in the growth models of Chapters 4 to 6. Money and prices do not enter those models. So for the quantity theory real GDP is given: $Y_t = \bar{Y}_t$.

**3. Constant velocity.** People's habits of paying, and the technology they pay with, change slowly. We take velocity as a constant: $V_t = \bar{V}$. It has no time subscript because it does not change over time.

**4. The central bank sets the money supply.** We do not model how the central bank decides; we take its choice as given: $M_t = \bar{M}_t$. (Chapter 12 gives monetary policy a richer model.)

| Equation | Name | What it takes as given |
|---|---|---|
| $M_tV_t = P_tY_t$ | quantity equation | none |
| $Y_t = \bar{Y}_t$ | classical dichotomy | $\bar{Y}_t$, from the growth models |
| $V_t = \bar{V}$ | constant velocity | $\bar{V}$ |
| $M_t = \bar{M}_t$ | money supply | $\bar{M}_t$, chosen by the central bank |

The endogenous variables are $M_t$, $V_t$, $P_t$ and $Y_t$. Three of the four equations simply set a variable equal to something given from outside.

<!-- cell -->

#### Solving the model

**Step 1: the price level.** Put the last three equations into the quantity equation (3):

$$\bar{M}_t\bar{V} = P_t\bar{Y}_t.$$

Only $P_t$ is unknown. Divide both sides by $\bar{Y}_t$:

$$P_t^* = \frac{\bar{M}_t\bar{V}}{\bar{Y}_t}. \tag{4}$$

The numerator, $\bar{M}_t\bar{V}$, is the spending power of the money in the economy; the denominator is the amount of goods there is to buy. The price level is their ratio. With $\bar{M} = 100$, $\bar{V} = 2$ and $\bar{Y} = 200$, $P^* = 100 \times 2/200 = 1$.

**Step 2: from levels to growth rates.** Inflation is the growth rate of $P$, so we turn equation (3) into growth rates. A product grows at a rate equal to its factors' growth rates added together ([Appendix C.5](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.5-growth-rates-and-the-growth-rules)). To see where that rule comes from, take logs of equation (3) in two years, $t$ and $t+1$:

$$\ln M_t + \ln V_t = \ln P_t + \ln Y_t, \qquad \ln M_{t+1} + \ln V_{t+1} = \ln P_{t+1} + \ln Y_{t+1}.$$

Subtract the first from the second. Each term becomes a change in a log, $\Delta \ln X = \ln X_{t+1} - \ln X_t$, and the change in a log is approximately the growth rate, $\Delta\ln X \approx g_X$ ([Appendix C.4](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.4-logarithms)). So money growth plus velocity growth equals inflation plus real GDP growth:

$$\bar{g}_M + \bar{g}_V = g_P + \bar{g}_Y. \tag{5}$$

**Step 3: inflation.** Velocity is constant, so $\bar{g}_V = 0$. Write $\pi = g_P$ and subtract $\bar{g}_Y$ from both sides of equation (5):

$$\pi^* = \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y. \tag{6}$$

Money that grows as fast as real GDP just keeps up with the extra goods; only the money growth beyond that raises prices. With $\bar{g}_M = 5$ and $\bar{g}_Y = 3$ percent, inflation is $5 - 3 = 2$ percent.

**How exact is the growth-rate rule?** In discrete time, write each variable in year $t+1$ as its value in year $t$ times one plus its growth rate, and divide equation (3) for year $t+1$ by equation (3) for year $t$:

$$\frac{M_{t+1}V_{t+1}}{M_tV_t} = \frac{P_{t+1}Y_{t+1}}{P_tY_t} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (1+\bar{g}_M)(1+\bar{g}_V) = (1+\pi)(1+\bar{g}_Y).$$

With $\bar{g}_V = 0$ the exact inflation rate is

$$\pi = \frac{1+\bar{g}_M}{1+\bar{g}_Y} - 1 = \frac{\bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y}{1+\bar{g}_Y}.$$

It differs from equation (6) only by the factor $1/(1+\bar{g}_Y)$, which is close to one. In our economy the exact rate is $1.05/1.03 - 1 = 1.94$ percent instead of 2 ([Appendix C.6](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.6-approximations)).

<!-- cell -->

#### What the model predicts

**Comparative statics.** Take logs of equation (4): $\ln P^* = \ln\bar{M} + \ln\bar{V} - \ln\bar{Y}$. Each coefficient is an elasticity, and they are all one in size. Equation (6) is already linear in growth rates, so its effects are one for one too.

| A change in ... | effect on the price level $P^*$ | effect on inflation $\pi^*$ | what moves in Figs. 3 and 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| money supply $\bar{M}$, up 1% once | $+1\%$ | none after that year | nothing |
| velocity $\bar{V}$, up 1% once | $+1\%$ | none after that year | nothing |
| real GDP $\bar{Y}$, up 1% once | $-1\%$ | none after that year | nothing |
| money growth $\bar{g}_M$, up 1 point | rises faster every year | $+1$ point | the economy moves along the line |
| real GDP growth $\bar{g}_Y$, up 1 point | rises more slowly | $-1$ point | the line $\pi = g_M - g_Y$ shifts down |
| velocity growth $\bar{g}_V$ (if not 0), up 1 point | rises faster | $+1$ point | points lie above the line |

A one-time change in a *level* gives a one-time jump in the price level; only a change in a *growth rate* changes inflation for good.

**Money growth drives inflation.** Real GDP growth comes from the slow forces of the growth models and stays in a narrow range, a few percent a year. Money growth is a policy choice and can be anything, from 2 percent to thousands of percent. So large and lasting differences in inflation, over time or across countries, must come from differences in money growth. That is the prediction Figs. 3 and 4 test.

**The neutrality of money.** Suppose the central bank multiplies the money supply by a factor $\lambda$, say $\lambda = 2$. By equation (4), with $\bar{V}$ and $\bar{Y}$ unchanged, the price level is multiplied by $\lambda$ too. If every price and every wage is multiplied by $\lambda$, then every *ratio* between them is unchanged:

$$\frac{\lambda p_{\text{bread}}}{\lambda p_{\text{book}}} = \frac{p_{\text{bread}}}{p_{\text{book}}}, \qquad \frac{\lambda W}{\lambda P} = \frac{W}{P}.$$

Relative prices and the real wage tell people what to buy, how much to work and what to produce, so no one has a reason to change what they do: real GDP stays at $\bar{Y}$. A change in the money supply that only changes nominal values is called **neutral**. The same algebra describes a currency reform that replaces every old note with $\lambda$ new ones. This is why the classical dichotomy is a good description of the long run.

**Only the long run.** In the short run, many prices and wages are slow to change. Then more money can change relative prices and real GDP for a while. The short-run model of Chapters 9 to 13 is built around that idea. The quantity theory is a theory of the long run.

<!-- cell -->

### Real and nominal interest rates: the Fisher equation

#### Assumptions

- A **nominal** interest rate $i$ is paid in dollars: put 1 dollar in the bank today and get $1+i$ dollars back next year. Banks and newspapers quote nominal rates.
- A **real** interest rate $R$ is paid in goods: give up 1 unit of goods today and get $1+R$ units next year. In the long run it equals the marginal product of capital, as in the [Solow model (Chapter 5)](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/ch05-the-solow-growth-model.html), so it is set by real forces, just like $\bar{Y}$.
- Prices rise at the rate $\pi$ between this year and the next: $P_{t+1} = (1+\pi)P_t$.

#### Solving the model

**Step 1: follow one dollar.** A saver can buy $1/P_t$ units of goods with 1 dollar today. If she saves the dollar instead, she gets $1+i$ dollars next year, which buy $(1+i)/P_{t+1}$ units of goods. Her return in goods is the ratio of the two:

$$1 + R = \frac{(1+i)/P_{t+1}}{1/P_t} = (1+i)\frac{P_t}{P_{t+1}} = \frac{1+i}{1+\pi}.$$

**Step 2: solve for the nominal rate.** Multiply both sides by $1+\pi$ and expand the product:

$$1 + i = (1+R)(1+\pi) = 1 + R + \pi + R\pi.$$

**Step 3: drop the small term.** At low rates, $R\pi$ is the product of two small numbers, tiny next to $R$ and $\pi$ themselves (2 percent times 2 percent is only 0.04 percent). Dropping it gives the **Fisher equation**:

$$i = R + \pi. \tag{7}$$

The nominal rate must pay the real return *and* make up for the fall in the value of the dollars being repaid. Subtracting $\pi$ from both sides gives the form we use with data:

$$R = i - \pi. \tag{8}$$

The real rate cannot be looked up; we compute it from a quoted nominal rate and measured inflation, as in Fig. 5. In our economy, $R = 2$ and $\pi = 2$ give $i = 4$ percent (the exact formula gives 4.04).

**Step 4: the long run.** Combine the Fisher equation (7) with the quantity theory (6):

$$i^* = R + \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y.$$

In the long run, $R$ is set by the marginal product of capital and $\bar{g}_Y$ by the growth models, so one more point of money growth raises the nominal interest rate by one point.

#### What the model predicts

| A change in ... | nominal rate $i$ | real rate $R$ |
|---|---|---|
| inflation $\pi$ up 1 point, $R$ given (long run) | $+1$ point | unchanged |
| inflation $\pi$ up 1 point, $i$ fixed in advance | unchanged | $-1$ point |
| real rate $R$ up 1 point, $\pi$ given | $+1$ point | $+1$ point |

- **High inflation, high nominal rates.** Countries and decades with high inflation should have high nominal interest rates, even if their real rates are normal.
- **Real rates can be negative.** If $i$ is below $\pi$, savers lose purchasing power. Equation (8) shows when that happens. A negative real rate could not last in the long run, because the marginal product of capital is positive. When we see one in the data, it tells us that the short run differs from the long run.
- **The shortcut fails at high inflation.** The exact rate is $R = (1+i)/(1+\pi) - 1$. With 14 percent nominal and 72 percent inflation, equation (8) gives $-58$ percent but the exact formula gives $-34$ percent ([Appendix C.6](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.6-approximations)).

<!-- cell -->

### Who gains and who loses from inflation

The book discusses the costs of inflation in words. The Fisher equation turns two of them into numbers.

#### Assumptions

- A lender and a borrower agree on a nominal rate $i$ for some years. They set it with the inflation they expect, $\pi^e$, so that $i = R^e + \pi^e$, where $R^e$ is the real rate they both want.
- Interest income is taxed at the rate $\tau$ on its *nominal* amount, as in most tax systems.

#### Solving the model

**A surprise.** Once the rate is fixed, the real rate the lender actually earns comes from equation (8) with the inflation that actually happens:

$$R = i - \pi = (R^e + \pi^e) - \pi = R^e - (\pi - \pi^e).$$

Every point of unexpected inflation, $\pi - \pi^e$, takes one point of real return from the lender and gives it to the borrower. In our economy the loan is set at $i = 2 + 2 = 4$ percent. If inflation turns out to be 8 percent, the lender earns $4 - 8 = -4$ percent in real terms, and the borrower repays with dollars worth less than expected.

**Taxes on nominal interest.** Now let inflation be expected, so that $i = R + \pi$, but the tax applies to all of $i$. The saver keeps $(1-\tau)i$ dollars of interest, and inflation still takes $\pi$, so her real return after tax is

$$(1-\tau)i - \pi = (1-\tau)(R + \pi) - \pi = (1-\tau)R - \tau\pi.$$

The last step multiplies out $(1-\tau)\pi - \pi = -\tau\pi$. The tax hits the part of the interest that only makes up for inflation as well. As a share of the real return $R$, the tax actually paid is $\tau R + \tau\pi$, an **effective tax rate** of $\tau(1 + \pi/R)$. With $\tau = 25$ percent and $R = 2$ percent, the effective rate is 50 percent at 2 percent inflation and 125 percent at 8 percent inflation, when the after-tax real return turns negative.

#### What the model predicts

- **Surprises redistribute.** Unexpected inflation moves wealth from lenders, savers and people on fixed nominal incomes to borrowers. Unexpected disinflation does the opposite. Expected inflation that is built into contracts does neither.
- **Inflation raises taxes on saving.** With taxes on nominal returns, higher inflation lowers the after-tax real return even when it is fully expected, which discourages saving and investment.
- **Indexing removes both effects.** Contracts, pensions and taxes written in real terms (adjusted for $\pi$) would make steady, known inflation little more than a nuisance. The real cost of inflation comes from surprises, and from rules written in dollars.

<!-- cell -->

### Seigniorage and the fiscal causes of high inflation

#### Assumptions

- The government spends $G$ dollars a year. It pays with taxes $T$, with new borrowing $\Delta B$ (the change in its debt $B$), or with new money $\Delta M$ (the change in the money stock $M$).
- The money in this block is the money the government itself issues: currency, or the monetary base. Its velocity $\bar{V}$ is nominal GDP divided by currency, about 12 for the United States in 2023.
- The quantity theory holds, with constant velocity.

#### Solving the model

**Step 1: the budget constraint.** Uses of funds equal sources of funds:

$$G = T + \Delta B + \Delta M. \tag{9}$$

Solved for the new money, $\Delta M = G - T - \Delta B$: whatever spending is not covered by taxes or new loans must be covered by printing money. The revenue from new money is called **seigniorage**, or the **inflation tax**.

**Step 2: seigniorage as a share of GDP.** Divide the new money by nominal GDP and write $\Delta M_t = \bar{g}_M M_{t-1}$, where $M_{t-1}$ is last year's stock. Since $M_t = (1+\bar{g}_M)M_{t-1}$ and, by the quantity equation (3), $M_t = P_tY_t/\bar{V}$,

$$\frac{\Delta M_t}{P_tY_t} = \frac{\bar{g}_M M_{t-1}}{P_tY_t} = \frac{\bar{g}_M}{1+\bar{g}_M}\cdot\frac{M_t}{P_tY_t} = \frac{\bar{g}_M}{(1+\bar{g}_M)\bar{V}}.$$

For low rates $1+\bar{g}_M \approx 1$, and the quantity theory (6) gives $\bar{g}_M = \pi^* + \bar{g}_Y$. So

$$\frac{\Delta M_t}{P_tY_t} = \frac{\bar{g}_M}{(1+\bar{g}_M)\bar{V}} \approx \frac{\pi^* + \bar{g}_Y}{\bar{V}}. \tag{10}$$

With 2 percent inflation, 3 percent real growth and $\bar{V} = 12$, new money pays for about $5/12 \approx 0.4$ percent of GDP a year.

**Step 3: who pays.** Split equation (10) into two parts. The part $\bar{g}_Y/\bar{V}$ is new money people want anyway, because a growing economy needs more money for its payments; it causes no inflation. The part $\pi^*/\bar{V}$ is a tax: every dollar people hold loses the share $\pi/(1+\pi)$ of its purchasing power each year, so the tax rate is about $\pi$ and the tax base is the real money people hold. Holders of currency pay it. People who hold land, houses or shares do not, because those prices rise along with all the others.

**Step 4: how much inflation a deficit needs.** Suppose lenders stop lending, $\Delta B = 0$, and taxes fall short of spending by a share $\sigma$ of GDP. Then equation (10) must equal $\sigma$. Multiply both sides by $(1+\bar{g}_M)\bar{V}$, collect the terms in $\bar{g}_M$, and solve ([Appendix C.9](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.9-solving-equations-and-systems)):

$$\sigma\bar{V}(1+\bar{g}_M) = \bar{g}_M \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sigma\bar{V} = \bar{g}_M(1 - \sigma\bar{V}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar{g}_M = \frac{\sigma\bar{V}}{1-\sigma\bar{V}}.$$

Inflation then follows from the exact quantity theory, $\pi = (1+\bar{g}_M)/(1+\bar{g}_Y) - 1$. A deficit of 5 percent of GDP with $\bar{V} = 12$ gives $\sigma\bar{V} = 0.6$, money growth of $0.6/0.4 = 150$ percent, and inflation of about 143 percent a year.

#### What the model predicts

- **Persistent high inflation is fiscal.** Rich countries raise well under 1 percent of GDP with new money, because inflation is low and people hold little currency. A government that loses access to taxes and loans must print money, and the quantity theory turns that money into inflation.
- **The printing press has a ceiling.** Since $\bar{g}_M/(1+\bar{g}_M) < 1$, seigniorage stays below $1/\bar{V}$ of GDP however fast money grows: about 8 percent of GDP with $\bar{V} = 12$. In practice the ceiling is lower, because people hold less money when it loses value fast, so velocity rises. A deficit close to the ceiling needs explosive money growth: this is the arithmetic of hyperinflation.
- **Ending a hyperinflation needs a fiscal fix.** Inflation falls when money growth falls, and by equation (9) money growth can fall only when spending falls, taxes rise or borrowing resumes. An **independent central bank**, one that the treasury cannot order to print, is a way to close the third option before a crisis.

### The model in code

We now turn the key results into Python functions. Each function's description names the equation it computes. The cells after it check the algebra above with numbers.

> **Python note.** `def` creates a *function*: a named recipe that takes inputs (the *arguments*) and
> gives back a result with `return`. Writing `g_V=0.0` gives an argument a *default value*, used
> whenever we do not pass one. All rates here are in percent.

```{python}
def price_level(M, V, Y):
    """Equation (4): the price level that solves the quantity equation M V = P Y."""
    return M * V / Y


def qt_inflation(g_M, g_Y, g_V=0.0):
    """Equations (5)-(6): inflation = money growth + velocity growth - real GDP growth (percent)."""
    return g_M + g_V - g_Y


def nominal_rate(R, pi):
    """Equation (7), the Fisher equation: the nominal interest rate i = R + pi (percent)."""
    return R + pi


def real_rate(i, pi):
    """Equation (8): the real interest rate R = i - pi (percent)."""
    return i - pi
```

**Check 1: measuring inflation.** Start a price index at 100 and let it grow by 2 percent a year for 35 years, using $P_{t+1} = (1+\pi)P_t$ from equation (1). The rule of 70 says it should about double. Then we recover the average rate from the two ends, and use equation (2) to convert a price and a fixed pension.

> **Python note.** An *f-string* such as `f"P = {P:.1f}"` inserts the value of a variable into a piece of
> text; `:.1f` means "one decimal" and `:+.1f` also prints the sign. `np.log` is the natural logarithm. `range(35)` counts 0, 1, ..., 34, so the
> `for` loop runs its indented line 35 times, and `P = P * 1.02` replaces the old value of `P` by the new one.

```{python}
P = 100.0
for year in range(35):
    P = P * 1.02                                  # one more year of 2% inflation
print(f"Price level after 35 years at 2%: {P:.1f}  (rule of 70: doubling in 70 / 2 = {70 / 2:.0f} years)")
print(f"Average inflation from the two ends: {100 * ((P / 100) ** (1 / 35) - 1):.3f}%")
print(f"Log shortcut, (ln P_T - ln P_0) / T:  {100 * (np.log(P) - np.log(100)) / 35:.3f}%")
print(f"A 50-dollar item at P = 100 costs {50 * 200 / 100:.0f} dollars at P = 200   (equation 2)")
print(f"A fixed pension of 1,000 dollars buys what {1000 * 100 / P:.0f} dollars bought 35 years earlier")
```

The log shortcut is slightly below 2 percent, because $\ln(1.02) = 0.0198$.

**Check 2: the price level and neutrality.** Equation (4) with our baseline should give $P^* = 1$. Raising
$\bar{M}$, $\bar{V}$ or $\bar{Y}$ by 1 percent should move $P^*$ by $+1$, $+1$ and $-1$ percent. And doubling money
should double every nominal value but leave the real wage alone.

```{python}
P_base = price_level(M=100, V=2, Y=200)
print(f"Baseline: P* = {P_base:.2f};  money doubled to 200: P* = {price_level(200, 2, 200):.2f}")
change_M = price_level(100 * 1.01, 2, 200) / P_base - 1
change_V = price_level(100, 2 * 1.01, 200) / P_base - 1
change_Y = price_level(100, 2, 200 * 1.01) / P_base - 1
print(f"1% more money:    P* changes by {100 * change_M:+.3f}%")
print(f"1% more velocity: P* changes by {100 * change_V:+.3f}%")
print(f"1% more real GDP: P* changes by {100 * change_Y:+.3f}%")
wage, bread = 30.0, 3.0                           # dollars per hour, dollars per loaf
print(f"Real wage before: {wage / bread:.0f} loaves an hour;  after doubling: {2 * wage / (2 * bread):.0f} loaves an hour")
```

The effect of real GDP is $-0.990$ rather than exactly $-1$ percent, because $1/1.01 = 0.990$: an elasticity
describes very small changes.

**Check 3: the growth-rate version.** We let money and real GDP grow year by year and solve equation (4) in
every year. Inflation should be the exact rate $1.05/1.03 - 1$, close to the shortcut of equation (6).

> **Python note.** `rows.append([...])` adds one row to a list, and `pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=[...])` turns
> the list into a table. `.pct_change()` gives the change from the previous row as a fraction, and
> `.iloc[-1]` picks the last row.

```{python}
def simulate_prices(g_M=5.0, g_Y=3.0, V=2.0, years=5):
    """Equation (4) year by year: money grows at g_M percent and real GDP at g_Y percent."""
    M, Y = 100.0, 200.0
    rows = []
    for t in range(years + 1):
        rows.append([t, M, Y, price_level(M, V, Y)])
        M = M * (1 + g_M / 100)
        Y = Y * (1 + g_Y / 100)
    path = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["year", "M", "Y", "P"])
    path["inflation"] = 100 * path.P.pct_change()
    return path


simulate_prices().round(3)
```

```{python}
for g_M in (5, 6, 100):
    simulated = simulate_prices(g_M=g_M).inflation.iloc[-1]
    exact = 100 * ((1 + g_M / 100) / 1.03 - 1)
    print(f"Money growth {g_M:3d}%: simulated {simulated:7.3f}%, exact {exact:7.3f}%, equation (6) {qt_inflation(g_M, 3):5.1f}%")
print(f"Velocity falling 1% a year, equation (5): inflation {qt_inflation(5, 3, g_V=-1):.1f}%")
```

Inflation is 1.942 percent in every year, not exactly 2, and one more point of money growth adds about one
point of inflation. For the moderate rates of Figs. 1 to 5 the shortcut is very close. For the hyperinflations
of Figs. 6 and 7 it is not (94 percent instead of 97 here), but the message is the same: more money growth,
more inflation.

**Check 4: the Fisher equation.** Follow one dollar as in step 1, and compare the shortcut of equations (7) and
(8) with the exact formula, at low and at very high inflation.

> **Python note.** `for i, pi in ((4, 2), (14, 72)):` walks through pairs of numbers: in the first round
> `i = 4` and `pi = 2`, in the second `i = 14` and `pi = 72`.

```{python}
goods_today = 100 / 1.00                          # 100 dollars at P = 1
goods_next_year = 100 * 1.04 / 1.02               # 104 dollars at P = 1.02
print(f"Exact real return on a 4% deposit with 2% inflation: {100 * (goods_next_year / goods_today - 1):.2f}%")
print(f"Equation (7), R = 2%, pi = 2%: i = {nominal_rate(2, 2):.1f}%;  exact (1+R)(1+pi) - 1 = {100 * (1.02 * 1.02 - 1):.2f}%")
for i, pi in ((4, 2), (14, 72)):
    exact = 100 * ((1 + i / 100) / (1 + pi / 100) - 1)
    print(f"i = {i}%, pi = {pi}%: R = {real_rate(i, pi):+.2f}% by equation (8), {exact:+.2f}% exact")
print(f"Long run, R = 2%: i* = {nominal_rate(2, qt_inflation(5, 3)):.0f}% with 5% money growth, "
      f"{nominal_rate(2, qt_inflation(6, 3)):.0f}% with 6%")
```

**Check 5: surprises and taxes.** A loan fixed at 4 percent loses its real value when inflation jumps. With a 25
percent tax on nominal interest, the after-tax real return computed directly must equal $(1-\tau)R - \tau\pi$.

```{python}
contract = nominal_rate(R=2, pi=2)                # set when everyone expects 2% inflation
for pi in (2, 8):
    print(f"Loan at {contract:.0f}%, inflation turns out {pi}%: real return {real_rate(contract, pi):+.1f}%")
tau, R = 0.25, 2
for pi in (2, 8):
    i = nominal_rate(R, pi)                       # expected inflation: i moves one for one
    after_tax = (1 - tau) * i - pi
    formula = (1 - tau) * R - tau * pi
    print(f"pi = {pi}%: i = {i}%, after-tax real return {after_tax:+.2f}% (formula {formula:+.2f}%), "
          f"effective tax rate {100 * (R - after_tax) / R:.0f}%")
```

**Check 6: seigniorage.** One year of our economy, now with currency as the money and $\bar{V} = 12$. The new
money as a share of GDP must match the exact formula in equation (10), and the shortcut should be close.

```{python}
V_cash = 12                                       # nominal GDP / currency
M, Y = 100.0, 1200.0                              # currency and real GDP: P = 100 x 12 / 1200 = 1
M_next, Y_next = M * 1.05, Y * 1.03               # one year of 5% money growth and 3% real growth
P_next = price_level(M_next, V_cash, Y_next)
direct = 100 * (M_next - M) / (P_next * Y_next)
exact = 100 * 0.05 / (1.05 * V_cash)
shortcut = (qt_inflation(5, 3) + 3) / V_cash
print(f"Price level next year: {P_next:.4f} (inflation {100 * (P_next - 1):.2f}%)")
print(f"New money: {direct:.3f}% of GDP directly, {exact:.3f}% exact, {shortcut:.3f}% by the shortcut")
```

**Check 7: financing a deficit with money.** Step 4 solved for the money growth that pays for a deficit of 5
percent of GDP. Putting that money growth back into equation (10) must return 5 percent. The last lines show
the ceiling $1/\bar{V}$.

```{python}
sigma = 0.05                                      # deficit to be paid with new money, share of GDP
g_M = sigma * V_cash / (1 - sigma * V_cash)
pi = (1 + g_M) / 1.03 - 1
print(f"Money growth needed: {100 * g_M:.0f}%;  inflation: {100 * pi:.0f}%")
print(f"Check, equation (10): new money = {100 * g_M / ((1 + g_M) * V_cash):.2f}% of GDP")
for growth_rate in (1.0, 10.0, 100.0):            # money growth of 100%, 1,000% and 10,000% a year
    share = 100 * growth_rate / ((1 + growth_rate) * V_cash)
    print(f"Money growth {100 * growth_rate:7,.0f}%: seigniorage {share:.2f}% of GDP")
print(f"Ceiling 1 / V: {100 / V_cash:.2f}% of GDP")
```

Even 10,000 percent money growth raises less than the ceiling of 8.33 percent of GDP, and only if velocity stayed
at 12. In a real hyperinflation people flee from money, velocity rises, and the ceiling falls.

### A color for every country

The textbook's figures show the United States and a few other countries. Every data figure of this notebook
lets you add more. A small file lists the World Bank's 217 economies, with their region, income group and
OECD membership:

```{python}
countries = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")
countries.head()
```

So that a country keeps its color from chart to chart, and two countries shown together never share one, we give
the colors with a small tool. Its palette has 44 colors: Plotly's 24 dark ones, and the 20 darker ones of its 26
"Alphabet" colors.

> **Python note.** `PALETTE = []` starts an empty list, and `.append` adds one color at a time. In `first_free`,
> `return` inside a loop stops the function at the first color that fits, `used.count(c)` counts how often `c`
> appears in the list `used`, and `reversed(PALETTE)` walks through the palette from its last color.

```{python}
LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]   # too pale on white
PALETTE = []
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24:                                       # 24 dark colors ...
    if c != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(c)
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:
    if c not in LIGHT:
        PALETTE.append(c)                                                     # ... and 20 more: 44 in all
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                    # a medium blue, too close to the U.S. navy: used last


def first_free(used, taken):
    """The palette color least used in `used` (the group-mates' colors), preferring one no country has `taken` yet."""
    for c in PALETTE:
        if c not in used and c not in taken:
            return c
    best = PALETTE[-1]
    for c in reversed(PALETTE):                  # from the end, far from the colors always on show
        if used.count(c) < used.count(best):
            best = c                             # a big group shares out the colors evenly
    return best
```

> **Python note.** `group_colors` walks through the countries one by one. `dict(fixed or {})` starts from a copy of
> the fixed colors (an empty dictionary when there are none), `continue` skips a country that already has a color,
> and `used` collects the colors of the countries that are shown together with this one.

```{python}
def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """Give each country a color that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    names: every country; groups: the lists of countries shown together (menu views); fixed: {country: color}
    for the textbook's countries, so the default view keeps the book's colors."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue
        used = []
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                for other in group:
                    if other in colors:
                        used.append(colors[other])
        colors[name] = first_free(used, list(colors.values()))
    return colors
```

Fig. 1's website version lists the G20 economies together, so no two of them share a color there. The textbook's
countries keep the chapter's own colors in every figure.

```{python}
BOOK_COLORS = {"United States": BLUE, "Argentina": TEAL, "Brazil": GREEN, "Russia": ORANGE, "Mexico": "#5aa0d8",
               "Nigeria": "#0b4f47", "Venezuela": "#b5651d"}
G20 = ["Argentina", "Australia", "Brazil", "Canada", "China", "France", "Germany", "India",
       "Indonesia", "Italy", "Japan", "Mexico", "Russia", "Saudi Arabia", "South Africa", "South Korea", "Turkey",
       "United Kingdom"]                          # with the United States and the European Union: the G20
INFLATION_COLORS = group_colors(sorted(countries.country), [G20 + ["United States"]], BOOK_COLORS)
print(INFLATION_COLORS["United States"], INFLATION_COLORS["Argentina"], INFLATION_COLORS["Japan"])
```

## Measuring inflation

We start with the facts: U.S. inflation since 1960, and the share of countries in the world with high inflation each year.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 1: The inflation rate in the United States

**Goal.** Follow U.S. inflation since 1960, and see how inflation rates add up to a much higher price level.

If $P_t$ is the price level in year $t$, the inflation rate is the percentage change
$(P_{t+1} - P_t)/P_t$ (equation 1). Here the price level is the **consumer price index** (CPI), the price of a basket
of consumer goods, averaged over the twelve months of each year.

> **Python note.** `pd.read_csv(...)` reads a data file into a *DataFrame*, a table with named columns.
> `.head()` shows its first five rows.

```{python}
us = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig8-1.csv")
us.head()
```

Inflation is the growth rate of the price level, so we can also go back from inflation to the price level.
Start at 100 in 1959 and multiply by $(1 + \pi_t/100)$ year after year.

> **Python note.** `.cumprod()` is the *cumulative product*: its first value is the first number, its
> second value the product of the first two numbers, and so on. `.tail()` shows the last five rows.

```{python}
us["price_level"] = 100 * (1 + us.inflation_cpi / 100).cumprod()
us.tail()
```

The United States is only one country. The World Bank's World Development Indicators (WDI) have the same
series, CPI inflation, for almost every economy, and a wider file has them for 200 economies since 1960:

```{python}
panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "inflation_panel.csv")
panel.head()
```

The column `source` says where each number comes from: `WDI` rows are the World Development Indicators, the data
behind Fig. 2, and `GID` rows fill gaps in the WDI from the World Bank's Global Inflation Database (we need them in
Figs. 6 and 7). Before mixing the two files, we compare the WDI's U.S. numbers with the textbook's series:

```{python}
wdi_us = panel[panel.country == "United States"].set_index("year").inflation
book_us = us.set_index("year").inflation_cpi
print(f"WDI: {wdi_us.index.min()}-{wdi_us.index.max()};  fig8-1.csv: {book_us.index.min()}-{book_us.index.max()}")
print(f"Largest difference in the years they share: {(wdi_us - book_us).abs().max():.2f} points")
```

They agree within 0.09 points, but the WDI stops in 2024. So we keep the textbook's U.S. series and take every
other country from the panel.

> **Python note.** `pd.concat([a, b])` stacks two tables that have the same columns. `sorted(...)` puts the
> names in alphabetical order, and `.unique()` lists each name once.

```{python}
us_rows = us[["year", "inflation_cpi"]].rename(columns={"inflation_cpi": "inflation"})
us_rows["country"] = "United States"
all_inflation = pd.concat([panel[panel.country != "United States"], us_rows], ignore_index=True)
CHOICES = sorted(all_inflation.country.unique())
print(len(CHOICES), "economies to choose from")
```

The chart has two views. The price level is shown on a **ratio scale**, where equal distances mean equal
*percentage* changes, so a steeper line means faster inflation. Each country's price level starts at 100 in the
year before its first inflation rate (1959 for the United States). Inflation rates differ hugely across countries,
so the top of the inflation axis moves up in steps (15, 30, 60, 120, 250, 500 percent) when a country needs it.

> **Python note.** `if ... else` runs one block of code or the other, and `return` inside a loop stops the
> function at the first match. With `log_y=True` the vertical axis is a ratio scale; `tickvals` chooses the
> numbers printed on it, and the `range` of a ratio axis is given in powers of 10 (`np.log10(80)`).

```{python}
PRICE_TICKS = [100, 200, 400, 800, 1600]
CAPS = [15, 30, 60, 120, 250, 500]               # possible tops of the inflation axis


def axis_top(value, caps):
    """The smallest number in caps that is at least value (the largest one if none is)."""
    for cap in caps:
        if value <= cap:
            return cap
    return caps[-1]


def price_index(rates):
    """Fig. 8.1: the price level implied by inflation rates (100 in the year before the first rate)."""
    return 100 * (1 + rates / 100).cumprod()
```

> **Python note.** `px.line(..., color="country")` draws one line per country, and
> `color_discrete_map=INFLATION_COLORS` fixes each country's color. `data.loc[data.inflation.idxmax()]` is the row
> with the highest inflation.

```{python}
def rate_view(data):
    """Fig. 8.1, inflation rates: one line per country; the top of the axis rises in steps."""
    top = axis_top(data.inflation.max(), CAPS)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=INFLATION_COLORS,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent)", "country": "Country"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=2))
    if data.country.nunique() == 1:
        fig.update_traces(fill="tozeroy")               # one country: an area chart, as in the textbook
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-2 * top / 15, top])
    peak = data.loc[data.inflation.idxmax()]
    title = f"{peak.country}: inflation peaked at {peak.inflation:,.1f}% in {peak.year:.0f}"
    if peak.inflation > top:
        title = f"{peak.country}: inflation peaked at {peak.inflation:,.0f}% in {peak.year:.0f} (axis cut at {top}%)"
    elif data.country.nunique() == 1:
        title = title + f"; {data.year.iloc[-1]}: {data.inflation.iloc[-1]:.1f}%"
    return fig, title
```

```{python}
def level_view(data):
    """Fig. 8.1, price levels on a ratio scale (100 in the year before each country's first rate)."""
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="price_level", color="country", log_y=True, hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=INFLATION_COLORS,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "price_level": "Price level (start = 100, ratio scale)", "country": "Country"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=3))
    top = data.price_level.max()
    if top < 1500:
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=PRICE_TICKS, range=[np.log10(80), np.log10(1500)])
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(dtick=1, exponentformat="power", range=[np.log10(80), np.log10(2 * top)])   # ticks 10², 10³, ...
    peak = data.loc[data.price_level.idxmax()]
    start = data[data.country == peak.country].year.min() - 1
    factor = f"{peak.price_level / 100:,.3g}" if peak.price_level < 1e8 else f"about 10^{np.log10(peak.price_level / 100):.0f}"
    return fig, f"{peak.country}: prices rose {factor}-fold from {start} to {peak.year:.0f}"
```

> **Python note.** `groupby("country").inflation.transform(price_index)` runs `price_index` separately on each
> country's rates and puts the results back in the original rows. `.copy()` makes a separate table, so that adding a
> column does not touch `all_inflation`.

```{python}
def inflation_chart(view="inflation rate", countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 8.1: CPI inflation, or the price level it adds up to, for the chosen countries."""
    if len(countries) == 0:
        countries = ("United States",)                 # nothing chosen: show the textbook's country
    data = all_inflation[all_inflation.country.isin(countries)].sort_values(["country", "year"]).copy()
    if view == "inflation rate":
        fig, title = rate_view(data)
    else:
        data["price_level"] = data.groupby("country").inflation.transform(price_index)
        fig, title = level_view(data)
    fig.update_layout(title=title, legend_title_text="")
    return fig
```

> **Python note.** `interact` calls the function and redraws its figure every time you change a widget.
> `ToggleButtons` shows one button per option, and the function receives the text of the chosen button.
> `SelectMultiple` is a list from which you can pick several countries: hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and click.
> The function receives the chosen names as a *tuple*, a list that cannot be changed. The `;` at the end only
> hides an extra line of text.

*On the website, click a country in the legend to add it (the G20 economies are listed; in Colab you can choose
any of the 200).*

**What to notice.**

- Inflation was low in the early 1960s, rose through the late 1960s and 1970s (the "Great Inflation"), and
  peaked at 13.5 percent in 1980.
- It fell sharply in the early 1980s, and from 1992 to 2020 it stayed below 4 percent. The Covid-19 years
  brought it back to 8.0 percent in 2022.
- In 2009 the rate was slightly negative: prices fell. That is **deflation**.
- Switch to the price level: prices are about 11 times their 1959 level. The line never falls for long,
  and it is steepest in the 1970s.
- Add Germany and Japan. The Great Inflation was a rich-world event, but its size differed: Germany peaked at
  only 7.0 percent in 1973, Japan at 23.2 percent in 1974. In the price-level view, Japan's line is almost flat
  from the mid-1990s to 2021: prices fell in 15 of those 27 years.

#### Key numbers: the Great Inflation and after

> **Python note.** `set_index("year")` uses the years as row labels, so `rate.loc[1960:1964]` keeps the
> rows from 1960 to 1964 and `rate[1980]` picks one number.


The textbook's numbers hold: about 1.3 percent a year in the early 1960s ("on the order of 2 percent"), a peak
of 13.50 percent in 1980, about 2 percent in 2000–2019, and 7.99 percent in 2022. By 2025 inflation was down
to 2.63 percent.

#### Table 8.1 and the case study "How much is that?"

How do we compare 27 cents in 1950 with \$3.50 in 2022? A longer CPI series, from MeasuringWorth, starts in
1774. Table 8.1 rescales it so that 2022 = 100; we add a column with the latest year, 2025, as the base.

```{python}
cpi = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "us_cpi.csv").set_index("year").cpi
years = [1900, 1930, 1950, 1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2022, 2025]
table = pd.DataFrame({"CPI, 2022 = 100": 100 * cpi[years] / cpi[2022],
                      "CPI, 2025 = 100": 100 * cpi[years] / cpi[2025]})
table["Textbook (2022 = 100)"] = [2.78, 5.71, 8.23, 10.12, 13.27, 28.15, 44.66, 58.84, 74.51, 100.00, None]
table.round(2)
```

Every cell of the textbook's table is reproduced. To move a price from one year to another, multiply by the
ratio of the two price levels: $0.27 \times 100/8.23$ for 1950 to 2022.

```{python}
def in_dollars_of(price, year, to_year=2025):
    """Table 8.1 case study: the value of `price` dollars of `year`, in dollars of `to_year`."""
    return price * cpi[to_year] / cpi[year]


print(f"27 cents of 1950 = {in_dollars_of(0.27, 1950, 2022):.2f} dollars of 2022 = {in_dollars_of(0.27, 1950):.2f} dollars of 2025")
print(f"Prices rose {100 * (cpi[2025] / cpi[2022] - 1):.1f}% from 2022 to 2025")
print(f"A 10,000-dollar pension of 1970 bought in 1983 what {in_dollars_of(10000, 1983, 1970):,.0f} dollars bought in 1970")
```

Gasoline at 27 cents in 1950 cost \$3.28 in 2022 dollars, just a little less than its 2022 price. The last line
is Mr. Gambino from the textbook's Section 8.4: a fixed pension of \$10,000 set in 1970 had lost 61 percent of
its value by 1983, and was worth about \$3,900 of 1970 dollars (the textbook says 40 percent, \$4,000).

### Fig. 2: The percentage of countries experiencing high inflation

**Goal.** See that high inflation was common around the world in the 1970s–1990s, and rare since 2000.

For each year, the textbook counts the share of countries with inflation above 25 percent. The file has this
share, and the number of countries with data in each year.

```{python}
high = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig8-2.csv")
high.head()
```

To try other thresholds we need the inflation rate of every country in every year: the panel of Fig. 1. To
redraw Fig. 8.2 we keep only its WDI rows, the data behind the textbook's figure.

> **Python note.** `panel[panel.source == "WDI"]` keeps the rows where the condition is true.
> `wdi.inflation > threshold` is a column of True/False values; its `.mean()` is the share of True values,
> because True counts as 1 and False as 0. `groupby(wdi.year)` computes this share separately for each year.

```{python}
wdi = panel[panel.source == "WDI"]
share_25 = 100 * (wdi.inflation > 25).groupby(wdi.year).mean()
print(f"Largest difference from fig8-2.csv: {(share_25.values - high.share_above_25_pct.values).max():.3f} points")
```

The threshold of 25 percent reproduces the file of Fig. 8.2. Was high inflation a worldwide event, or did it hit
some regions more than others? With the region of every economy from `countries.csv` we can compute the same share
for a **group** of economies: the World Bank's seven regions, or the OECD members.

> **Python note.** `.isin(codes)` is True for the rows whose code is in `codes`. `.size()` counts the rows of each
> group: here, the number of economies with data in each year.

```{python}
GROUPS = ["World", "OECD members"] + sorted(countries.region.unique())
GROUP_COLORS = group_colors(GROUPS, [GROUPS], {"World": BLUE})   # the World keeps the textbook's blue


def group_share(threshold, group):
    """Fig. 8.2: the percentage of a group's reporting economies with inflation above `threshold`, by year."""
    if group == "World":
        members = countries.iso3
    elif group == "OECD members":
        members = countries.iso3[countries.oecd]
    else:
        members = countries.iso3[countries.region == group]
    sub = wdi[wdi.iso3.isin(members)]
    share = (100 * (sub.inflation > threshold).groupby(sub.year).mean()).reset_index(name="share")
    share["economies"] = sub.groupby("year").size().values
    share["group"] = group
    return share
```

```{python}
def high_inflation_share(threshold=25, groups=("World",)):
    """Fig. 8.2: the percentage of economies with inflation above `threshold` percent, for each group."""
    if len(groups) == 0:
        groups = ("World",)                             # nothing chosen: the textbook's view
    tables = []
    for group in groups:
        tables.append(group_share(threshold, group))
    shares = pd.concat(tables)
    first = shares[shares.group == groups[0]]
    peak = first.loc[first.share.idxmax()]
    fig = px.line(shares, x="year", y="share", color="group", hover_name="group", hover_data=["economies"],
                  color_discrete_map=GROUP_COLORS, labels={"year": "Year", "share": "Fraction of countries (percent)"},
                  title=f"Inflation above {threshold}%: {groups[0]} peaked at {peak.share:.1f}% in {peak.year:.0f}")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=2))
    if len(groups) == 1:
        fig.update_traces(fill="tozeroy")               # one group: an area chart, as in the textbook
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 104], tickvals=[20, 40, 60, 80, 100])   # no label in the bottom-left corner
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig
```

> **Python note.** A `Dropdown` is a menu: the function receives the option you pick.

**What to notice.**

- With the textbook's threshold of 25 percent, the share was small in the 1960s, jumped in 1974, stayed
  high in the 1980s and peaked in 1994, when almost one country in three had high inflation.
- After the mid-1990s the share collapsed. The Covid-19 years brought a small rise, and by 2025 it was down
  to 3 percent.
- Choose 10 percent: in 1974, most countries had double-digit inflation. Choose 100 percent: inflation of
  that size never hit more than about one country in nine, and it peaked in the early 1990s.
- Add the regions: high inflation came in waves. In Latin America & Caribbean the share reached 41 percent in 1974
  and 39 percent in 1991; in Europe & Central Asia it peaked at 40.5 percent in 1993, the years after the Soviet
  Union broke up; in Sub-Saharan Africa it jumped to 55.6 percent in 1994, when the CFA franc of West and Central
  Africa was devalued by half. Hover over a line to see how many economies are behind each share: North America
  and South Asia have only a handful, so their shares jump in big steps.

## Testing the quantity theory

The quantity theory predicts that faster money growth goes with higher inflation. We check it twice, with U.S. decades and with a cross-section of economies.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 3: Money growth and inflation in the United States

**Goal.** Test the main prediction of the quantity theory with U.S. history: periods of fast money growth
should be periods of high inflation.

Each point is one decade. Money is **M2** (currency, checking accounts, savings deposits and money market
accounts; see Table 8.2 below). Both growth rates are average annual rates from the first year of a decade
to the first year of the next:

$$g = \left(\frac{X_{d+10}}{X_d}\right)^{1/10} - 1$$

```{python}
decades = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig8-3.csv")
decades.tail()
```

The last row covers only 2020–2025, a decade that is not over yet. To choose other period lengths, and other
countries, we load yearly data on money and prices. The Jordà–Schularick–Taylor **Macrohistory Database** has broad
money and the CPI for 18 rich economies since 1870. For the United States the file splices it with M2 from the
Federal Reserve after 1958, exactly the series behind `fig8-3.csv`.

```{python}
money_panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "money_prices_panel.csv")
money_panel.groupby("country").year.agg(["min", "max", "count"]).T
```

`money` and `cpi` are indexes in each country's own units, so only their growth rates can be compared across
countries. Two things to notice: the other countries stop in 2020, and some have gaps. Germany has no money data
for 1923–1924 (the hyperinflation) and 1939–1947 (the war), and Belgium's money starts in 1979.

> **Python note.** `range(1870, last, years)` counts 1870, 1870 + years, ... up to the year before `last`: the
> first year of each period. `min(a, b)` is the smaller number, so the last period stops at the last year of data.
> `x ** (1 / n)` is the n-th root. `and` is True only when both conditions are.

```{python}
def growth(x, start, end):
    """Average annual growth of x from start to end, in percent."""
    return 100 * ((x[end] / x[start]) ** (1 / (end - start)) - 1)


def periods(years=10, country="United States"):
    """Fig. 8.3: average money growth and inflation in periods of `years` years since 1870, for one country."""
    data = money_panel[money_panel.country == country].set_index("year")
    last = data.index.max()
    rows = []
    for start in range(1870, last, years):
        end = min(start + years, last)
        if start in data.index and end in data.index:      # skip periods that start or end in a gap
            label = f"{start}s" if (years == 10 and end - start == 10) else f"{start}–{end}"
            if end - start < years:
                label = label + "*"                       # * marks an unfinished period
            rows.append([country, label, start, end, growth(data.money, start, end), growth(data.cpi, start, end)])
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["country", "period", "start", "end", "money_growth", "inflation"])


check = periods(10)
print(f"Largest difference from fig8-3.csv: {(check.money_growth - decades.money_growth).abs().max():.3f} (money), "
      f"{(check.inflation - decades.inflation).abs().max():.3f} (inflation)")
```

The quantity theory says $\pi = g_M + g_V - g_Y$. If velocity were constant and real GDP did not grow, every
point would lie on the 45-degree line $\pi = g_M$. Real GDP does grow, so points should lie **below** that line,
by about $g_Y - g_V$. The chart draws both lines; the lower one is shifted down by the average gap in the data.

Germany's 1920s are a problem for any chart: money grew by more than 1,000 percent a year *on average over the
decade*. The axes widen once (to 70 percent) when a country needs it, and points beyond that are listed in a note
instead of squeezing all the others into a corner.

> **Python note.** `.between(a, b)` is True for values from a to b. `table.drop(shown.index)` keeps the rows that
> are *not* in `shown`. `.corr()` is the *correlation* of two columns: 1 for points on a rising straight line, 0 for
> no relation.

```{python}
KEY_DECADES = ["1870s", "1930s", "1940s", "1970s", "1980s", "2010s", "2020–2025*"]
JST_COUNTRIES = sorted(money_panel.country.unique())
MONEY_COLORS = group_colors(JST_COUNTRIES, [JST_COUNTRIES], BOOK_COLORS)   # the website lists all 18 together


def period_table(years, countries):
    """Fig. 8.3: the periods of all chosen countries, split into points on the chart and points beyond 70%."""
    tables = []
    for country in countries:
        tables.append(periods(years, country))
    table = pd.concat(tables, ignore_index=True)
    inside = table.money_growth.between(-10, 70) & table.inflation.between(-10, 70)
    us_key = (table.country == "United States") & (table.period.isin(KEY_DECADES) | (years == 20))
    table["label"] = table.period.where(us_key, "")   # labels for the textbook's decades; hover shows the rest
    return table[inside], table[~inside]
```

```{python}
def add_reference_lines(fig, xr, gap, off):
    """Fig. 8.3: the 45-degree line, the quantity-theory line pi = g_M - gap, and a note on points off the chart."""
    g_M = np.array(xr)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=g_M, y=g_M, mode="lines", name="π = g_M (45-degree line)", line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dot")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=g_M, y=qt_inflation(g_M, gap), mode="lines", name=f"π = g_M − {gap:.1f}",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY, line_width=1)
    notes = []
    for row in off.itertuples():
        notes.append(f"{row.country} {row.period}: money {row.money_growth:,.0f}%, inflation {row.inflation:,.0f}%")
    if len(notes) > 0:
        fig.add_annotation(x=0.01, y=0.98, xref="paper", yref="paper", xanchor="left", yanchor="top", align="left",
                           showarrow=False, text="Off the chart:<br>" + "<br>".join(notes), font=dict(size=12))
```

```{python}
def money_and_prices(years=10, countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 8.3: money growth against inflation, one point per period of `years` years and country."""
    shown, off = period_table(years, countries if len(countries) > 0 else ("United States",))
    gap = (shown.money_growth - shown.inflation).mean()
    r = shown.money_growth.corr(shown.inflation)
    fig = px.scatter(shown, x="money_growth", y="inflation", color="country", text="label", hover_name="period",
                     hover_data=["country"], color_discrete_map=MONEY_COLORS,
                     labels={"money_growth": "Money growth (percent per year)", "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent per year)"},
                     title=f"{years}-year periods: correlation {r:.2f}, average gap g_M − π = {gap:.1f} points")
    fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=11), textposition="top center", textfont=dict(size=11))
    wide = shown.money_growth.max() > 18 or shown.inflation.max() > 17 or shown.inflation.min() < -5
    xr, yr = ([-8, 70], [-10, 70]) if wide else ([-3, 18], [-5, 17])   # widen once, when a country needs it
    if wide:
        fig.update_traces(mode="markers")             # zoomed out, the decade labels would pile up: hover instead
    add_reference_lines(fig, xr, gap, off)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=xr)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=yr)
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.15, yanchor="top"), legend_title_text="")
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(money_and_prices,
         years=Dropdown(options=[5, 10, 20], value=10, description="years per period", style=WIDE),
         countries=SelectMultiple(options=JST_COUNTRIES, value=["United States"], rows=6, description="countries"));
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: Fig. 3 with a precomputed slider for the length of the periods and 17 more countries
def money_website(years):
    """Website: the textbook's U.S. figure, plus the other 17 countries' periods (hidden until clicked)."""
    fig = money_and_prices(years)
    tables = []
    for country in JST_COUNTRIES:
        if country != "United States":
            tables.append(periods(years, country))
    extra = px.scatter(pd.concat(tables), x="money_growth", y="inflation", color="country", hover_name="period",
                       hover_data=["country"], color_discrete_map=MONEY_COLORS)
    for t in extra.data:
        fig.add_trace(t.update(marker_size=9))
    return fig


book_names = []
for t in money_and_prices(10).data:
    book_names.append(t.name)
fig = slider_figure(money_website, "years", [5, 10, 20], start=10, label="years per period")
legend_only(fig, book_names)
fig.update_xaxes(autorange=True)                    # the axes fit the countries you switch on
fig.update_yaxes(autorange=True)
fig.update_layout(height=600)                       # room for the legend below the plot ...
fig.layout.sliders[0].pad.t = 140                   # ... and for the slider below the legend
fig
```

**Sources.** Data: [Jordà–Schularick–Taylor Macrohistory Database, release 6, broad money (`money`) and the CPI (`cpi`)](https://www.macrohistory.net/database/)
(Jordà, Schularick and Taylor 2017), 18 economies, 1870–2020; for the United States since 1959,
[Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, M2 (`M2NS`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/M2NS),
and [MeasuringWorth, Officer and Williamson, The Annual Consumer Price Index for the United States, 1774–Present](https://www.measuringworth.com/datasets/uscpi/).
Prepared files: [`data/ch08/fig8-3.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch08/fig8-3.csv) and [`data/ch08/money_prices_panel.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch08/money_prices_panel.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch08/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 8.3 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

*On the website, click a country in the legend to add its periods; the numbers in the title are for the United
States. Germany's 1920s lie far outside the chart: double-click the plot to zoom back out after adding Germany.*

**What to notice.**

- With decades, as in the textbook, the 1910s and the 1970s have the fastest inflation and fast money growth.
  The 1920s and 1930s had slow money growth and **deflation**: prices fell.
- The points rise from left to right, roughly parallel to the 45-degree line, and about 4 points below it.
  The quantity theory says this gap is the growth of real GDP minus the growth of velocity.
- With 5-year periods the cloud is wider. Wars and the Great Depression move prices a lot over a few years,
  and the theory is about the long run. Hover over the points to see the periods.
- With 20-year periods there are only 8 points, all with money growth between 5 and 9 percent.
- Add Japan, Italy and France. Their 1940s, the war years, sit far up and to the right (Japan: money growth 45 percent
  and inflation 65 percent a year), and the axes widen to show them: they lie on the same band as everything else. Add
  Germany: its 1920s are listed in the note, because money grew 1,139 percent a year and prices 1,210 percent.
  Select all 18 countries: the correlation of the 10-year points is 0.86, and the average gap is 4.0 points, the same
  as in the United States alone.

<!-- cell -->

#### Table 8.2: measures of the money supply

What counts as money? The narrowest measure is **currency**. The **monetary base** adds the reserves banks
hold at the central bank, **M1** adds checking accounts, and **M2** adds savings and money market accounts.
A monthly file from the Federal Reserve has all four, in billions of dollars.

> **Python note.** `parse_dates=["date"]` turns text such as `"2023-01-01"` into real dates.
> `.loc[[...]]` picks rows by their labels, and `.T` *transposes* the table: rows become columns.
> `{last:%B %Y}` prints a date as "August 2026".

```{python}
supply = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "money_supply.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).set_index("date")
last = supply.index[-1]
table = supply.loc[[pd.Timestamp("2023-01-01"), last]].T
table.columns = ["January 2023", f"{last:%B %Y}"]
table["Textbook (Jan. 2023)"] = [2300, 5300, 19600, 21300]
table.round(0)
```

January 2023 reproduces the textbook's table within its rounding. Something odd stands out: M1 is almost as
large as M2. Look at the spring of 2020:

```{python}
supply.loc["2020-03":"2020-07"]
```

M1 more than triples between April and May 2020, from 4,856 to 16,313 billion dollars. Nobody printed 11
trillion dollars that month: in May 2020 the Federal Reserve changed the definition of M1 and moved savings
deposits into it. A jump like this is a **series break**. Growth rates across the break are meaningless, which
is one reason Fig. 3 uses M2, whose definition did not change.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: is velocity constant?

The quantity theory assumes a constant velocity. The quantity equation, equation (3), lets us measure it:
$V = PY/M$, nominal GDP divided by money. A small annual file has nominal GDP, currency and M2.

```{python}
yearly = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "us_money_annual.csv").set_index("year")
yearly["velocity"] = yearly.nominal_gdp / yearly.m2
fig = px.line(yearly.reset_index(), x="year", y="velocity", hover_name="year",
              labels={"year": "Year", "velocity": "Velocity of M2 (nominal GDP / M2)"},
              title="M2 velocity stayed near 1.8 until about 1990, then rose and fell")
fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3))
fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 2.5], tickvals=[0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5])   # no label in the bottom-left corner
fig.show()
print(yearly.velocity.loc[[1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 1997, 2007, 2021, 2025]].round(2).to_dict())
```

**Sources.** Data: [U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Gross Domestic Product (`GDPA`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPA);
[Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, M2 (`M2SL`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/M2SL), calendar-year averages.
Prepared file: [`data/ch08/us_money_annual.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch08/us_money_annual.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch08/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by the discussion of velocity in Chapter 8 of Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612), which has no figure of it.

<!-- cell -->

From 1960 to 1990, M2 velocity stayed between about 1.7 and 1.9, close to the textbook's assumption. Then it rose
to 2.18 in 1997 and fell to 1.16 in 2021, when savings piled up during the pandemic. When velocity falls, money
can grow faster than nominal GDP without extra inflation: in equation (5) $\bar{g}_V$ is negative.

### Fig. 4: Money growth and inflation around the world

**Goal.** Test the quantity theory across countries: economies where money grows fast should have high inflation.

Each row is one economy. The columns are average annual money growth (broad money) and average annual
inflation, in percent, for two periods: the textbook's 1990–2021 and the latest 1990–2025.

```{python}
world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig8-4.csv")
world.head()
```

The `n_` columns count the years behind each average, and `n_infl_filled` the years of inflation taken from the
Global Inflation Database because the WDI no longer has them. Three steps of data hygiene were already done when
the file was built: aggregates such as "World" were removed, economies with fewer than 5 years were dropped, and
a few broad-money **series breaks** (a currency reform shows up as money "growth" of over 100,000 percent) were
deleted. One country is new compared with the textbook:

```{python}
world[world.iso3.isin(["VEN", "COD", "GEO", "BRA", "JPN", "CHE"])][["country", "money_growth_1990_2025", "inflation_1990_2025",
                                                                     "n_money_1990_2025", "n_infl_1990_2025"]]
```

Venezuela's average inflation of 2,614 percent is not an error: it is the hyperinflation of 2017–2021 (Fig. 7),
which is not in the textbook's data. Unlike Venezuela's GDP numbers in earlier chapters, these numbers are real,
so we keep Venezuela and label it.

Inflation ranges from under 1 to over 2,000 percent, so both axes use a ratio scale, as in the textbook. We
label a few economies; hover over any point to see its name and how many years of data are behind its two averages.

> **Python note.** `.map(LABELS)` replaces each code with its label from the dictionary `LABELS`; codes that
> are not in it become empty (`NaN`), and `.fillna("")` turns those into empty text. `np.geomspace(a, b, 200)`
> gives 200 numbers from `a` to `b` that are evenly spaced on a ratio scale.

```{python}
LABELS = {"JPN": "Japan", "CHE": "Switzerland", "DNK": "Denmark", "TUR": "Turkey", "ARG": "Argentina",
          "RUS": "Russia", "GEO": "Georgia", "BRA": "Brazil", "AGO": "Angola", "COD": "Congo, Dem. Rep.",
          "VEN": "Venezuela", "UKR": "Ukraine"}
world["label"] = world.iso3.map(LABELS).fillna("")
POSITIONS = {"COD": "middle left", "BRA": "bottom right", "AGO": "top left"}   # labels that would be cut off or overlap
world["position"] = world.iso3.map(POSITIONS).fillna("middle right")
MONEY_TICKS = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512]
INFLATION_TICKS = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048]   # no label in the bottom-left corner
```

```{python}
def world_money(g_Y=3.0, period="1990–2025"):
    """Fig. 8.4: average money growth and inflation by economy, with the line pi = g_M - g_Y."""
    suffix = period.replace("–", "_")
    x, y, n_m, n_p = "money_growth_" + suffix, "inflation_" + suffix, "n_money_" + suffix, "n_infl_" + suffix
    above = (world[y] > qt_inflation(world[x], g_Y)).sum()
    fig = px.scatter(world, x=x, y=y, text="label", hover_name="country", log_x=True, log_y=True,
                     hover_data=[n_m, n_p],                       # years behind each average, shown on hover
                     labels={x: f"Money growth, {period} average (percent, ratio scale)",
                             y: "Inflation rate (percent, ratio scale)",
                             n_m: "years of money data", n_p: "years of inflation data"},
                     title=f"π = g_M − g_Y with g_Y = {g_Y:.0f}%: {above} of {len(world)} economies lie above the line")
    fig.update_traces(marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=8), textposition=list(world.position), textfont=dict(color=BLUE, size=11))
    g_M = np.geomspace(g_Y + 0.4, 900, 200)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=g_M, y=qt_inflation(g_M, g_Y), mode="lines", name=f"Quantity theory, π = g_M − {g_Y:.0f}",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=MONEY_TICKS, range=[np.log10(1.5), np.log10(900)])
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=INFLATION_TICKS, range=[np.log10(0.3), np.log10(4000)])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.02, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom"))
    return fig
```

Move the slider to change the growth rate of real GDP in the quantity-theory line, and switch between the two periods.

```{python}
         g_Y=FloatSlider(value=3, min=0, max=8, step=1, description="real GDP growth g_Y (percent)", style=WIDE),
         period=ToggleButtons(options=["1990–2025", "1990–2021"], description="period"));
```

```{python}
# @title Website version: Fig. 4 with a precomputed slider for real GDP growth in the quantity-theory line
slider_figure(world_money, "g_Y", [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], start=3, label="real GDP growth g_Y (percent)")
```

**Sources.** Data: [World Bank, World Development Indicators, Broad money growth (`FM.LBL.BMNY.ZG`)](https://databank.worldbank.org/metadataglossary/world-development-indicators/series/FM.LBL.BMNY.ZG);
[World Bank, World Development Indicators, Inflation, consumer prices (`FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG`)](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG), with gaps filled from the [World Bank's Global Inflation Database](https://www.worldbank.org/en/research/brief/inflation-database) (Ha, Kose and Ohnsorge 2023).
Prepared file: [`data/ch08/fig8-4.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch08/fig8-4.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch08/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 8.4 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- The economies line up along a rising band: the faster money grows, the higher inflation. Brazil, Angola and
  the Democratic Republic of the Congo have both money growth and inflation in the hundreds of percent.
- Most economies sit in the dense cloud at the lower left, with money growth of about 10–20 percent and inflation
  of about 3–18 percent (the middle half of each column, printed below). Japan and Switzerland are near the bottom.
- With $g_Y = 0$ the line is the 45-degree line: most economies lie below it, because real GDP grows. On a ratio
  scale, subtracting $g_Y$ bends the line down a lot at low money growth and hardly at all at high money growth.
- Georgia and Venezuela lie far above the band, for a statistical reason. Look at the `n_` columns above: their
  money averages cover fewer years than their inflation averages. In the World Bank data, Georgia's money series
  starts in 1996, after its hyperinflation, and Venezuela's stops in 2013, before its hyperinflation. An average
  of inflation over crisis years compared with an average of money growth over calm years is not a fair test.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: how well does the quantity theory fit?

> **Python note.** `np.log10` takes logarithms, the numbers behind a ratio scale. The correlation of the logs
> measures how close the points are to a straight line on the chart.

```{python}
for period in ["1990_2021", "1990_2025"]:
    g, p = world["money_growth_" + period], world["inflation_" + period]
    print(f"{period}: correlation of the logs {np.log10(g).corr(np.log10(p)):.2f}; "
          f"median gap g_M - pi {(g - p).median():.1f} points; inflation above money growth in {(p > g).sum()} economies")
print("Middle half of money growth:", world.money_growth_1990_2025.quantile([0.25, 0.75]).round(1).tolist(),
      " of inflation:", world.inflation_1990_2025.quantile([0.25, 0.75]).round(1).tolist())
textbook = world.set_index("country").loc[["Denmark", "Switzerland", "Turkiye", "Argentina"]]
textbook[["money_growth_1990_2021", "inflation_1990_2021"]].round(1)
```

The textbook's examples hold in the 1990–2021 averages: Denmark and Switzerland had inflation of 1.8 and 1.0
percent with money growth of about 4–5 percent, while Turkey and Argentina averaged above 25 percent for both.
(The World Bank now spells Turkey "Turkiye".) The correlation of the logs is 0.85 in both periods, and the
median economy has money growth 5.6 to 5.8 points above inflation. With constant velocity this gap would be the growth
rate of real GDP; a gap this large suggests that velocity fell in many economies, as it did in the United States after 1997.
