## Real and nominal interest rates

The Fisher equation subtracts inflation from the interest rate a bank pays to get the real return, which is what matters for saving and borrowing.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 5: Real and nominal interest rates in the United States

**Goal.** Use the Fisher equation to turn a nominal interest rate into a real one.

The nominal rate is the return on 3-month U.S. Treasury bills, averaged over each year. The real rate cannot be
looked up: we compute it with equation (8), $R = i - \pi$, using the CPI inflation of Fig. 1.

```{python}
rates = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig8-5.csv")
rates.head()
```

The file already has a `real_rate` column. Let us check it with our function `real_rate` from "Model overview".

```{python}
R = real_rate(rates.nominal_tbill_3m, rates.inflation_cpi)
print(f"Largest difference from the file's real rate: {(R - rates.real_rate).abs().max():.3f} points")
```

The same calculation works for any country with a short-term interest rate. A wider file has 3-month rates for
50 economies (the OECD members and several large emerging economies), with each country's CPI inflation from the
panel of Fig. 1:

```{python}
rates_panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "interest_rates_panel.csv")
rates_panel[rates_panel.year == 2024].head()
```

`rate_source` says where the rate comes from. For the United States it is the Treasury-bill rate of the textbook.
For the other countries it is the OECD's 3-month money-market (interbank) rate, a rate at which banks lend to each
other. That is a slightly different rate: in the United States the OECD's 3-month rate has been 0.6 points above the
Treasury-bill rate on average.

Before plotting, we give the columns readable names for the legend. Inflation is hidden at first; click it in
the legend to show it. Hover over the chart to read all three numbers of a year and check that $i = R + \pi$.
Rates in some countries were much higher than in the United States, so the vertical axis widens in steps.

```{python}
RATE_RANGES = [[-10, 16], [-20, 32], [-40, 64], [-80, 128], [-200, 250]]


def rate_range(low, high):
    """The first range in RATE_RANGES that contains both low and high (the widest one if none does)."""
    for bottom, top in RATE_RANGES:
        if bottom <= low and high <= top:
            return [bottom, top]
    return RATE_RANGES[-1]
```

```{python}
def interest_rates(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 8.5: the nominal rate i, the real rate R = i - pi and inflation pi of one country."""
    data = rates_panel[rates_panel.country == country]
    named = data.rename(columns={"short_rate": "Nominal rate, i", "real_rate": "Real rate, R = i − π",
                                 "inflation": "Inflation, π"})
    negative = (data.real_rate < 0).sum()
    fig = px.line(named, x="year", y=["Nominal rate, i", "Real rate, R = i − π", "Inflation, π"], hover_name="year",
                  color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN, ORANGE], labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent"},
                  title=f"{country}: the real rate R = i − π was negative in {negative} of {data.real_rate.count()} years")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=3))
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Inflation, π"), visible="legendonly", line=dict(dash="dot"))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    yr = rate_range(data[["short_rate", "inflation", "real_rate"]].min().min(),
                    data[["short_rate", "inflation", "real_rate"]].max().max())
    fig.update_yaxes(range=yr, tickvals=[-5, 0, 5, 10, 15] if yr == [-10, 16] else None)   # no label in the corner
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1959, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified", legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.15, yanchor="top"), legend_title_text="")
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(interest_rates, country=Dropdown(options=sorted(rates_panel.country.unique()), value="United States",
                                          description="country", style=WIDE));
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: Fig. 5 with a menu of 50 countries
RATE_COUNTRIES = sorted(rates_panel.country.unique())
figures = {}
for c in RATE_COUNTRIES:
    figures[c] = interest_rates(c)
fig = go.Figure(layout=figures["United States"].layout)
owner = []
for c in RATE_COUNTRIES:
    for t in figures[c].data:
        if c != "United States":
            t.visible = False
        fig.add_trace(t)
        owner.append(c)
buttons = []
for c in RATE_COUNTRIES:
    shown = []
    for o, t in zip(owner, fig.data):
        shown.append(("legendonly" if t.name == "Inflation, π" else True) if o == c else False)
    lay = figures[c].layout
    buttons.append(dict(label=c, method="update", args=[{"visible": shown}, {
        "title.text": lay.title.text, "yaxis.range": list(lay.yaxis.range), "yaxis.tickvals": lay.yaxis.tickvals}]))
fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=RATE_COUNTRIES.index("United States"), x=0.01, y=0.98,
                                    xanchor="left", yanchor="top")])
fig
```

**Sources.** Data: for the United States,
[Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 3-Month Treasury Bill Secondary Market Rate (`TB3MS`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/TB3MS)
and [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (`CPIAUCSL`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCSL); for the other economies, the 3-month interest rate from the
[OECD Data Explorer](https://data-explorer.oecd.org/): Economic Outlook No. 119, short-term interest rate (`IRS`,
dataflow `DSD_EO@DF_EO`), with earlier years from the OECD's financial-market statistics, 3-month interbank rate
(`IR3TIB`, dataflow `DSD_STES@DF_FINMARK`; also on FRED, e.g. [Germany, `IR3TIB01DEM156N`](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IR3TIB01DEM156N)),
and inflation from [World Bank, World Development Indicators, Inflation, consumer prices (`FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG`)](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG) and the [World Bank's Global Inflation Database](https://www.worldbank.org/en/research/brief/inflation-database) (Ha, Kose and Ohnsorge 2023).
Prepared files: [`data/ch08/fig8-5.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch08/fig8-5.csv) and [`data/ch08/interest_rates_panel.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch08/interest_rates_panel.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch08/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 8.5 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

*On the website, choose a country in the menu at the top left.*

**What to notice.**

- The nominal rate is high when inflation is high. It peaked at just over 14 percent in 1981, a year after
  inflation peaked.
- The real rate was negative in the 1970s, in most years since 2008, and sharply negative in 2021–2022, when
  inflation jumped while the nominal rate was still near zero.
- In 2009 the real rate was **above** the nominal rate. Show inflation in the legend: it was negative that year.
- Choose Germany. In 1974 the U.S. real rate was −3.2 percent, but Germany's was +2.9 percent: its central bank
  fought the inflation of the 1970s earlier and harder, and German inflation never went above 7 percent (Fig. 1).
- Choose Turkey: in 2022 its short rate was 14 percent and inflation 72 percent, a real rate of −58 percent by
  $R = i - \pi$. With rates this high the shortcut is poor; the exact real rate, $(1+i)/(1+\pi) - 1$, is −34 percent.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: real rates

```{python}
r = rates.set_index("year")
print(f"Highest nominal rate: {r.nominal_tbill_3m.max():.1f}% in {r.nominal_tbill_3m.idxmax()}")
print(f"2009: nominal {r.nominal_tbill_3m[2009]:.2f}%, inflation {r.inflation_cpi[2009]:.2f}%, real {r.real_rate[2009]:.2f}%")
print("Years with a negative real rate:", r.index[r.real_rate < 0].tolist())
print(f"Lowest real rate: {r.real_rate.min():.2f}% in {r.real_rate.idxmin()};  {r.index[-1]}: {r.real_rate.iloc[-1]:.2f}%")
print(f"Average real rate: 1960-2022 {r.real_rate.loc[:2022].mean():.2f}%, 1960-2007 {r.real_rate.loc[:2007].mean():.2f}%")
```

Most of the textbook's statements hold: a nominal peak of 14.0 percent in 1981, a real rate above the nominal
rate in 2009, negative real rates in 2003 and in every year from 2010 to 2018, and −5.97 percent in 2022. One does
not: the textbook says the real rate averages "about 1.5 percent" over the period, but the plotted series averages
0.59 percent over 1960–2022 (1.31 percent over 1960–2007). Since 2023 the real rate has been positive again.

## Hyperinflation and high inflation

Finally, the extreme cases: inflation of hundreds or thousands of percent a year, why it starts and how it can end.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 6: Hyperinflations in Argentina, Brazil, and Russia

**Goal.** See how extreme inflation can get, and how quickly a hyperinflation can end.

A **hyperinflation** is inflation above about 500 percent a year. The textbook's file has annual CPI inflation for
three countries that went through one, and the file of Fig. 8.7 three more. We load both now, because Figs. 6
and 7 share one table.

```{python}
hyper = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig8-6.csv")
hyper = hyper.rename(columns={"argentina": "Argentina", "brazil": "Brazil", "russia": "Russia"})
latam = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig8-7.csv")
latam = latam.rename(columns={"mexico": "Mexico", "nigeria": "Nigeria", "venezuela": "Venezuela"})
hyper.head()
```

Two gaps, compared with the textbook: the World Bank no longer publishes Argentina's inflation before 1970, so the
line starts in 1970; and Argentina before 2018 comes from the Global Inflation Database, because the WDI has dropped
those years. Brazil starts in 1981 and Russia in 1993.

<!-- cell -->

#### Data hygiene: Zimbabwe

Every other country comes from the panel of Fig. 1. Before using it, look at one country the textbook mentions,
Zimbabwe, whose hyperinflation peaked in November 2008:

```{python}
panel[(panel.country == "Zimbabwe") & (panel.year >= 2000) & (panel.year <= 2009)]
```

These numbers cannot be right. They say that prices **fell** by 73 percent in 2007 and rose only 157 percent in 2008,
when, according to the textbook, prices were doubling roughly every day. Zimbabwe's official price statistics broke
down during the crisis, and no reliable annual series exists. We drop Zimbabwe's values for 2001–2008. (The same years
enter Zimbabwe's average in Fig. 4, so its point there is not reliable either.)

> **Python note.** `~` means "not": `panel[~bad]` keeps every row where `bad` is False. `.melt(id_vars="year", ...)`
> turns the country columns of the textbook's files into rows, one row per country and year, the shape of the panel.
> `HIGH` lists Fig. 7's countries (peaks of 100 to 500 percent, `|` adds the textbook's three), and `PATH_COLORS`
> gives the countries of each list different colors.

```{python}
bad = (panel.country == "Zimbabwe") & (panel.year >= 2001) & (panel.year <= 2008)
clean = panel[~bad]
book = pd.concat([hyper.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="country", value_name="inflation"),
                  latam.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="country", value_name="inflation")]).dropna()
paths = pd.concat([book, clean[~clean.country.isin(book.country.unique())]], ignore_index=True)   # textbook files, then the panel
peaks = paths.groupby("country").inflation.max()
HYPER = sorted(peaks[peaks > 500].index)
HIGH = sorted(set(peaks[(peaks > 100) & (peaks <= 500)].index) | {"Mexico", "Nigeria", "Venezuela"})   # Fig. 7's list
PATH_COLORS = group_colors(sorted(paths.country.unique()), [HYPER, HIGH], BOOK_COLORS)
print(len(HYPER), "economies with at least one year above 500%:", HYPER)
```

On a linear scale, the peaks of thousands of percent flatten everything else. A ratio scale shows every level of
inflation at once, but it cannot show zero or negative rates: Argentina's deflation of 2001 (−1.1 percent) simply
leaves a gap. The axes widen when a country with a higher peak is added.

```{python}
RATIO_TICKS = [0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000, 30000, 100000]   # no label in the bottom-left corner
LINEAR_TICKS = [500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000]                            # (the textbook's linear scale)
LINEAR_TOPS = [3500, 7000, 15000, 75000]


def disinflation(data):
    """Figs. 8.6-8.7: the highest peak among the chosen countries, and when that country fell below 25%."""
    top = data.loc[data.inflation.idxmax()]
    own = data[data.country == top.country]
    later = own[(own.year > top.year) & (own.inflation < 25)]
    if len(later) > 0:
        return f"{top.country}: {top.inflation:,.0f}% in {top.year:.0f}, below 25% by {later.year.min():.0f}"
    return f"{top.country}: {top.inflation:,.0f}% in {top.year:.0f}, still above 25% in {own.year.max():.0f}"
```

```{python}
def inflation_paths(countries=("Argentina", "Brazil", "Russia"), scale="linear"):
    """Figs. 8.6 and 8.7: inflation in the chosen countries, on a linear or a ratio scale."""
    data = paths[paths.country.isin(countries if len(countries) > 0 else ("Argentina",))]
    title = disinflation(data)
    if scale == "ratio":
        data = data[data.inflation > 0]                  # a ratio scale cannot show zero or falling prices
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", log_y=(scale == "ratio"), hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=PATH_COLORS, title=title,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent)", "country": "Country"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=3))
    fig.add_hline(y=500, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY, annotation_text="500%: hyperinflation",
                  annotation_position="bottom left")
    peak = data.inflation.max()
    if scale == "ratio":
        top = 5000 if peak < 5000 else 200000
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=RATIO_TICKS, range=[np.log10(0.1), np.log10(top)])
    else:
        top = axis_top(1.1 * peak, LINEAR_TOPS)
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=LINEAR_TICKS if top == 3500 else None, range=[-top / 35, top])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1960, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified", legend_title_text="")
    return fig
```

> **Python note.** Several widgets in one `interact` call: each argument of the function gets its own widget.

```{python}
interact(inflation_paths, countries=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(paths.country.unique()), value=["Argentina", "Brazil", "Russia"],
                                                   rows=8, description="countries"),
         scale=ToggleButtons(options=["linear", "ratio"], description="vertical scale"));
```

```{python}

# @title Website version: Fig. 6 with buttons for the vertical scale and the 31 hyperinflations in the legend
fig = inflation_paths(HYPER, "linear")
fig.update_layout(title=inflation_paths(("Argentina", "Brazil", "Russia"), "linear").layout.title)   # the title of the default view
legend_only(fig, ["Argentina", "Brazil", "Russia"])
fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=[1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020])   # no year label in the bottom-left corner
scale_buttons(fig, RATIO_TICKS, start="linear")
```

#### The inflation tax

Why would a government let money grow so fast? Because printing money is one way to pay its bills. The
**government budget constraint** says that spending $G$ is paid with taxes $T$, new borrowing $\Delta B$, or new
money $\Delta M$ (equation 9):

$$G = T + \Delta B + \Delta M$$

The revenue from new money is called **seignorage**, or the **inflation tax**. It is paid by everyone who holds
money: when the price level doubles, a 200-dollar bill buys only what 100 dollars bought before.

```{python}
def money_printed(G, T, dB):
    """Equation (9): the new money the government must issue, Delta M = G - T - Delta B."""
    return G - T - dB


print(f"Spending 25% of GDP, taxes 20%, new borrowing 2%: new money = {money_printed(25, 20, 2):.0f}% of GDP")
print(f"If lenders stop lending (new borrowing 0%):        new money = {money_printed(25, 20, 0):.0f}% of GDP")
print(f"Real value of 200 dollars of currency after prices double: {200 / 2:.0f} dollars of today")
```

In the United States, the inflation tax is tiny. Measured as new currency issued each year, as a percentage of GDP:

> **Python note.** `.diff()` gives the change from the previous row: here, the currency added in each year.

```{python}
yearly["new_currency"] = 100 * yearly.currency.diff() / yearly.nominal_gdp
print(yearly.new_currency.loc[[1975, 1980, 2000, 2020, 2025]].round(2).to_dict())
print(f"Largest: {yearly.new_currency.max():.2f}% of GDP in {yearly.new_currency.idxmax()}")
```

Even in the Great Inflation, new currency brought in about 0.4 percent of GDP, and the largest value since 1960 is
under 1 percent of GDP, in 2020. The textbook reports that countries with high inflation typically raise about 5 percent
of GDP or less this way, and Argentina more than 10 percent in the late 1970s and early 1980s. That is why Thomas Sargent
calls persistent high inflation "a fiscal phenomenon".

## Concluding remarks

- Inflation is the growth rate of the price level, equation (1). U.S. inflation peaked at 13.5 percent in 1980, stayed
  near 2 percent for two decades, and jumped to 8 percent in 2022. A price index turns past prices into today's dollars,
  equation (2), and at 2 percent a year prices double in about 35 years.
- The quantity theory of money adds three assumptions to the quantity equation (3) and solves for the price level,
  $P^* = \bar{M}\bar{V}/\bar{Y}$, equation (4), and for inflation, $\pi^* = \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y$, equations (5) and (6):
  in the long run, faster money growth means higher inflation, one for one, and money is neutral. U.S. decades and
  165 economies line up as predicted, although velocity is not really constant.
- The Fisher equation, $i = R + \pi$, equations (7) and (8), turns nominal interest rates into real ones. U.S. real
  rates were negative in the 1970s and in most years since 2008. Surprise inflation moves wealth from lenders to
  borrowers, and taxes on nominal interest make inflation a tax on saving.
- The government budget constraint, equation (9), shows why governments print money, and equation (10) how much
  revenue it raises: well under 1 percent of GDP in the United States, and, with constant velocity, never more than $1/\bar{V}$ of GDP.
  Hyperinflations happen when governments cannot pay their bills with taxes or borrowing: persistent high inflation
  is a fiscal problem. They can end as quickly as they start.
- The next chapter starts the short-run part of the book, with an introduction to economic fluctuations.

### Conceptual problems

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 1 (Basic): Turkey drops six zeros.** On 1 January 2005, Turkey replaced its currency with the new Turkish
lira, worth 1,000,000 old liras ([European Central Bank](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/policy_and_exchange_rates/euro_reference_exchange_rates/html/eurofxref-graph-trl.en.html)).
Overnight, every banknote, price, wage, bank balance and debt was divided by one million.

(a) In equation (4), divide the money supply $\bar{M}$ by 1,000,000 and keep $\bar{V}$ and $\bar{Y}$ as they are. What
happens to the price level $P^*$?

(b) Take some made-up round numbers: a worker earns 600 million old liras a month, and a kilo of bread costs 1.5
million old liras. What is her real wage, in kilos of bread a month, before and after the reform?

(c) In our data, Turkish inflation was 8.6 percent in 2004 and 8.2 percent in 2005. Use equation (6) to explain why
the reform by itself could not lower inflation. What would have to change instead?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

The reform is the neutrality experiment of the Model overview, with $\lambda = 1/1{,}000{,}000$. For (c), look at the
variables in equation (6): are they levels or growth rates?

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Equation (4) says $P^* = \bar{M}\bar{V}/\bar{Y}$. Put $\bar{M}/1{,}000{,}000$ in place of $\bar{M}$:

$$P^*_{\text{new}} = \frac{(\bar{M}/1{,}000{,}000)\,\bar{V}}{\bar{Y}} = \frac{P^*}{1{,}000{,}000}.$$

The price level is divided by one million as well: bread at 1,500,000 old liras costs 1.5 new liras.

**(b)** Before the reform: $600{,}000{,}000 / 1{,}500{,}000 = 400$ kilos a month. After it: $600 / 1.5 = 400$ kilos.
The real wage is unchanged, and so is every relative price. Nobody has a reason to work, buy or produce differently,
so real GDP stays at $\bar{Y}$: the reform is **neutral**.

**(c)** Equation (6), $\pi^* = \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y$, contains growth rates, not levels. Dividing the money stock by
one million in every year leaves its growth rate as it was:

$$\frac{M_{t+1}/10^6 - M_t/10^6}{M_t/10^6} = \frac{M_{t+1} - M_t}{M_t}.$$

So inflation stayed where money growth put it: 8.6 percent in 2004, 8.2 percent in 2005 and 9.6 percent in 2006. To
lower inflation, money growth has to slow down, and by equation (9) that needs a budget that does not lean on new
money. In Turkey the big fall had come before the reform, from 45.0 percent in 2002 to 21.6 percent in 2003 and 8.6
percent in 2004 (our data). The new lira mainly made prices easier to read, write and compute.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 2 (Intermediate): The 3 percent mortgage of 2021.** In 2021 the average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate
mortgage in the United States was 2.96 percent ([Freddie Mac, Primary Mortgage Market Survey (`MORTGAGE30US`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/MORTGAGE30US)),
and the Federal Reserve aims for inflation of [2 percent over the longer run](https://www.federalreserve.gov/faqs/economy_14400.htm)
(it measures inflation with another price index, but the CPI is close enough here). Suppose a family and its bank
both expected 2 percent inflation when they signed such a mortgage in 2021. CPI inflation then turned out as in Fig. 1:

| | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CPI inflation (percent) | 4.68 | 7.99 | 4.13 | 2.95 |

(a) What real interest rate did both sides expect?

(b) What real rate did the bank actually earn in 2022, and in 2023? How many points of real return moved from the bank
to the family in each of these years?

(c) The family owes 300,000 dollars and, to keep things simple, repays none of it before 2024. By how much did the
price level rise from 2021 to 2024? What was the debt worth in 2021 dollars in 2024, and what would it have been
worth with 2 percent inflation in each year?

(d) Who gained and who lost from the surprise? Why would a family whose mortgage rate follows market interest rates
(an adjustable-rate mortgage) have gained less?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

For (a) and (b), use equation (8) and the formula for a surprise in "Who gains and who loses from inflation". For (c),
the rate for 2022 is the rise of the price level from 2021 to 2022, so chain the rates of 2022, 2023 and 2024 as in
the Model overview, then use equation (2).

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** By equation (8), the real rate both sides expected was $R^e = i - \pi^e = 2.96 - 2 = 0.96$ percent.

**(b)** The real rate the bank earned is $R = i - \pi$: in 2022, $2.96 - 7.99 = -5.03$ percent; in 2023,
$2.96 - 4.13 = -1.17$ percent. With $R = R^e - (\pi - \pi^e)$, the surprise moved $7.99 - 2 = 5.99$ points of real
return from the bank to the family in 2022, and $4.13 - 2 = 2.13$ points in 2023. The exact real rates,
$(1+i)/(1+\pi) - 1$, are −4.66 and −1.12 percent: at these rates the shortcut works well.

**(c)** The price level of 2024 is that of 2021 times one plus each year's inflation rate:

```python
price_rise = (1 + 0.0799) * (1 + 0.0413) * (1 + 0.0295)    # P_2024 / P_2021
on_target = 1.02 ** 3                                        # three years at 2%
print(f"Price level: +{100 * (price_rise - 1):.1f}% (on target: +{100 * (on_target - 1):.1f}%)")
print(f"Debt in 2021 dollars: {300000 / price_rise:,.0f} (on target: {300000 / on_target:,.0f})")
```

Prices rose by 15.8 percent from 2021 to 2024, against 6.1 percent on the 2 percent path. By equation (2), the debt of
300,000 dollars was worth 259,141 dollars of 2021 in 2024, against 282,697 dollars with 2 percent inflation. The surprise
took 23,556 dollars of real value off the debt.

**(d)** The family, and every borrower at a fixed nominal rate, gained. The bank, and anyone who held fixed-rate loans
or bonds, lost: they were repaid in dollars that buy less. With an adjustable rate, the family's interest rate rises
when market rates rise, and by the Fisher equation (7) market rates rise with inflation. So its real rate falls by
less: the surprise moves wealth only while the nominal rate is fixed in advance.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 3 (Challenge): Should the inflation target be 4 percent?** In 2010, three IMF economists asked whether
central banks should aim for 4 percent inflation instead of 2 percent, so that interest rates would be higher in normal
times and could be cut further in a deep recession ([Blanchard, Dell'Ariccia and Mauro 2010](https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/spn/2010/spn1003.pdf)).
Weigh the idea for the United States with the chapter's equations. Assume a long-run real interest rate of $R = 1$
percent and real GDP growth of $\bar{g}_Y = 2$ percent (round numbers for this problem, not estimates).

(a) How many years does the price level take to double at 2 percent and at 4 percent inflation? Use the rule of 70,
then the exact formula.

(b) Use equation (7) to find the long-run nominal interest rate under each target. In 2007–2008 the Federal Reserve
cut its policy rate: the federal funds rate fell from 5.26 percent in July 2007 to 0.16 percent in December 2008 ([Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Funds Effective Rate (`FEDFUNDS`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS)).
Which target leaves room for a cut of about that size before the rate reaches zero?

(c) Use equation (10) to compute seigniorage under each target, with the velocity of U.S. currency in 2025 from our
data, $\bar{V} = 12.9$. How much extra revenue, as a percentage of GDP, would the higher target bring?

(d) The switch takes the holders of 10-year bonds by surprise: they bought them when everyone expected 2 percent. By
how many points does their real return fall each year? By what percentage does the real value of their final payment
fall?

(e) Weigh (a) to (d). Would you support the higher target? Name one cost of inflation from the chapter that these
numbers leave out.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

For (a), use the doubling-time step of the Model overview, $T\ln(1+\pi) = \ln 2$. For (c), the shortcut in equation
(10) is enough. For (d), a bond pays a fixed number of dollars, so the real value of its final payment depends on how
far the price level has risen after 10 years under each inflation rate.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The rule of 70 gives $70/2 = 35$ years at 2 percent and $70/4 = 17.5$ years at 4 percent. The exact doubling
time is $T = \ln 2/\ln(1+\pi)$: $0.6931/0.0198 = 35.0$ years and $0.6931/0.0392 = 17.7$ years. At 4 percent, prices
double twice as fast.

**(b)** By equation (7), $i^* = R + \pi$: $1 + 2 = 3$ percent under the 2 percent target and $1 + 4 = 5$ percent under
the 4 percent target (the exact formula gives 3.02 and 5.04 percent). The cut of 2007–2008 was $5.26 - 0.16 = 5.10$
points. With a nominal rate of 3 percent, the central bank can cut by only 3 points before it reaches zero; with 5
percent it can cut by 5 points, almost all of the 5.10 points it used in 2007–2008.

**(c)** With the shortcut of equation (10), seigniorage is $(\pi + \bar{g}_Y)/\bar{V}$:

$$\frac{2 + 2}{12.9} = 0.31 \text{ percent of GDP}, \qquad \frac{4 + 2}{12.9} = 0.47 \text{ percent of GDP}.$$

The higher target brings in about 0.16 percent of GDP more each year (0.14 percent with the exact formula). That is a
small gain.

**(d)** The bonds pay a nominal rate fixed for 2 percent inflation. By $R = R^e - (\pi - \pi^e)$, their real return
falls by $4 - 2 = 2$ points each year. After 10 years, the final payment buys

$$\left(\frac{1.02}{1.04}\right)^{10} = 0.824$$

times what the holders expected: 17.6 percent less. The holders' loss is the gain of whoever issued the bonds, often
the government itself.

**(e)** For the higher target: two more points of room to cut rates in a deep recession, and a little more revenue.
Against it: prices double in about 18 years instead of 35, so everything fixed in dollars (wages in contracts, pensions,
savings in cash) loses value twice as fast; the switch takes 17.6 percent of the real value of existing 10-year bonds
from their holders; and people may wonder whether 4 percent is the last increase. Costs left out of (a) to (d)
include the higher tax on saving when taxes apply to nominal interest (Problem 9), and the cost of rules and contracts
written in dollars. Reasonable people disagree: an answer that weighs the room to cut rates against these costs, with
numbers, is a good answer.

</details>

**Problem 4 (Basic): A worldwide surge in 2022.** Was the inflation of 2022 a U.S. story? Use `inflation_panel.csv`,
the panel of Fig. 1 (CPI inflation from the [World Bank's World Development Indicators](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG),
with gaps filled from the [World Bank's Global Inflation Database](https://www.worldbank.org/en/research/brief/inflation-database)),
and the OECD members marked in `countries.csv` (from the [OECD's list of members](https://www.oecd.org/en/about/members-partners.html)).

(a) Compute the median inflation rate of the 38 OECD members in each year from 2017 to 2025. In which year did it
peak, and at what rate?

(b) How many members had inflation above 5 percent in 2019, and how many in 2022?

(c) Which four members had the highest inflation in 2022, and which two the lowest? Where does the United States rank?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Keep the panel's rows whose `country` is one of `countries.country[countries.oecd]` (use `.isin(...)`), then use
`groupby("year")` and `.median()`. For (c), sort the rows of 2022 with `.sort_values("inflation")`.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Read both files, keep the OECD members, take the median of each year, count the members above 5 percent, and sort the
rows of 2022:

```python
inflation_rows = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "inflation_panel.csv")
members = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")
oecd_inflation = inflation_rows[inflation_rows.country.isin(members.country[members.oecd])]
print(oecd_inflation.groupby("year").inflation.median().loc[2017:].round(2).to_dict())
for year in (2019, 2022):
    one_year = oecd_inflation[oecd_inflation.year == year]
    print(year, ":", (one_year.inflation > 5).sum(), "of", len(one_year), "members above 5%")
in_2022 = oecd_inflation[oecd_inflation.year == 2022].sort_values("inflation", ascending=False)
print(in_2022[["country", "inflation"]].head(4).round(1).to_string(index=False))
print(in_2022[["country", "inflation"]].tail(2).round(1).to_string(index=False))
print("Rank of the United States, from the top:", list(in_2022.country).index("United States") + 1)
```

- **(a)** The median was below 2 percent from 2017 to 2020 (1.74 percent in 2019, 0.73 percent in 2020) and 2.82
  percent in 2021. It peaked at 8.24 percent in 2022, then fell to 5.68 percent in 2023 and 2.77 percent in 2024.
  The 2025 median, 2.84 percent, covers 37 members: the panel has no U.S. value for 2025 yet.
- **(b)** In 2019 only 1 member of 38 had inflation above 5 percent (Turkey, at 15.2 percent); in 2022, 35 of 38 did.
- **(c)** The highest rates in 2022 were Turkey's 72.3 percent, then Lithuania's 19.7, Estonia's 19.4 and Latvia's 17.3
  percent. The lowest were Japan's 2.5 and Switzerland's 2.8 percent. The United States, at 8.0 percent, ranks 21st of
  38 from the top, close to the median.

The surge was almost everywhere at once. Causes that hit many countries together are a topic for the short-run model of
Chapters 9 to 13; the quantity theory is about the long run.

</details>

**Problem 5 (Intermediate): Do high-inflation countries pay higher interest rates?** If real interest rates are similar
across countries, the Fisher equation (7) predicts that economies with higher inflation have higher nominal interest
rates, point for point. Test it with `interest_rates_panel.csv`, the 50 economies of Fig. 5 (3-month rates from the
[OECD Data Explorer](https://data-explorer.oecd.org/), and for the United States the Treasury-bill rate,
[`TB3MS`, via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/TB3MS)).

(a) Keep the years 2000–2019. Compute each economy's average short rate, average inflation rate and average real rate.

(b) Compute the correlation between average inflation and the average short rate, and the slope of a straight line
through the points. Is the slope close to 1?

(c) Which three economies had the highest average real rates, and which three the lowest?

(d) Several economies have exactly the same average short rate, 1.69 percent. How many, which ones, and why? What does
that mean for their real rates?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

`groupby("country")[["short_rate", "inflation", "real_rate"]].mean()` gives one row per economy.
`np.polyfit(x, y, 1)` returns the slope and the intercept of the best straight line. For (d), keep the rows whose
average short rate, rounded to two decimals, equals 1.69, and look at the list of names.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Average each economy's rows over 2000–2019, then compare the columns:

```python
rates_rows = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "interest_rates_panel.csv")
rates_2000_2019 = rates_rows[(rates_rows.year >= 2000) & (rates_rows.year <= 2019)]
averages = rates_2000_2019.groupby("country")[["short_rate", "inflation", "real_rate"]].mean()
print(len(averages), "economies")
print(f"Correlation: {averages.inflation.corr(averages.short_rate):.2f}")
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(averages.inflation, averages.short_rate, 1)
print(f"Slope {slope:.2f}, intercept {intercept:.2f}")
by_real_rate = averages.real_rate.sort_values()
print("Lowest:", by_real_rate.head(3).round(2).to_dict())
print("Highest:", by_real_rate.tail(3).round(2).to_dict())
same_rate = averages[averages.short_rate.round(2) == 1.69]
print(len(same_rate), "economies at 1.69%:", list(same_rate.index))
print(same_rate.sort_values("inflation")[["inflation", "real_rate"]].round(2))
```

- **(b)** Across the 50 economies the correlation is 0.93, and the slope is 1.19: one more point of average inflation
  goes with about 1.2 more points of nominal interest. The prediction holds well. The slope is a little above 1
  because some high-inflation economies also had high real rates.
- **(c)** The highest average real rates were Brazil's 6.77 percent, Turkey's 5.23 and Iceland's 3.42 percent. The
  lowest were Russia's −1.50, Estonia's −1.03 and Bulgaria's −0.98 percent. Some economies have fewer years in the
  window (for example Turkey from 2002 and Costa Rica from 2011).
- **(d)** Eleven economies share 1.69 percent: Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg,
  the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain. They are the 11 countries whose central banks handed monetary policy to the
  [European Central Bank](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/ecb/orga/escb/html/index.en.html) in 1999, so they share one
  euro money-market rate. (Greece joined in 2001, so its average differs a little.) One nominal rate with different
  inflation rates means different real rates: from −0.41 percent in Spain to +0.26 percent in France. By equation (8),
  the members with the highest inflation had the lowest real rates.

</details>

**Problem 6 (Intermediate): Where did the money of 2020 go?** U.S. M2 grew by 19.1 percent in 2020 and by 16.1
percent in 2021, and inflation peaked in 2022. Use `us_money_annual.csv` (nominal GDP from the
[Bureau of Economic Analysis, `GDPA`, via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPA), and M2 from the
[Federal Reserve, `M2SL`, via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/M2SL)) and the CPI in `us_cpi.csv`
([MeasuringWorth](https://www.measuringworth.com/datasets/uscpi/)).

(a) Compute the yearly growth rates of M2, nominal GDP and velocity, $V = PY/M$, for 2019 to 2025.

(b) In growth rates, equation (3) says that money growth plus velocity growth equals the growth of nominal GDP. Check
it for 2020 and 2023, first with the shortcut $g_M + g_V$, then with the exact form $(1+g_M)(1+g_V) - 1$.

(c) Compare the total growth of M2, nominal GDP, velocity and the CPI over the six years from 2019 to 2025.

(d) What do your numbers say about the quantity theory's assumption of a constant velocity, from year to year and over
the six years as a whole?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

After `set_index("year")`, `.pct_change()` gives every column's growth rate in one step. For (b), the shortcut is the
growth-rate rule of the Model overview, which assumes small changes. For (c), divide the value of 2025 by the value of
2019.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Compute velocity, then the growth rates; check the identity; and compare 2025 with 2019:

```python
money_years = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "us_money_annual.csv").set_index("year")
money_years["velocity"] = money_years.nominal_gdp / money_years.m2
growth_rates = 100 * money_years[["m2", "nominal_gdp", "velocity"]].pct_change()
print(growth_rates.loc[2019:2025].round(2))
for year in (2020, 2023):
    m2_growth, gdp_growth, v_growth = growth_rates.loc[year] / 100
    print(f"{year}: shortcut {100 * (m2_growth + v_growth):.2f}%, exact {100 * ((1 + m2_growth) * (1 + v_growth) - 1):.2f}%, "
          f"nominal GDP {100 * gdp_growth:.2f}%")
cpi_years = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "us_cpi.csv").set_index("year").cpi
for name, series in (("M2", money_years.m2), ("nominal GDP", money_years.nominal_gdp),
                     ("velocity", money_years.velocity), ("CPI", cpi_years)):
    print(f"{name}: {100 * (series[2025] / series[2019] - 1):+.1f}% from 2019 to 2025")
```

- **(a)** Velocity fell by 16.65 percent in 2020 and 4.28 percent in 2021, then rose again: by 4.31 percent in 2022 and
  10.55 percent in 2023, when M2 *fell* by 3.42 percent (the only fall in this file, which starts in 1959).
- **(b)** In 2020 the shortcut gives $19.06 - 16.65 = 2.41$ percent, but nominal GDP fell by 0.76 percent. The exact
  form gives $1.1906 \times 0.8335 - 1 = -0.76$ percent, as it must: the quantity equation is an identity, and the
  shortcut fails for changes this large. In 2023 the shortcut gives 7.14 percent and the exact form 6.78 percent, the
  growth of nominal GDP.
- **(c)** From 2019 to 2025, M2 grew by 47.8 percent, nominal GDP by 43.3 percent and the CPI by 25.9 percent, while
  velocity ended only 3.0 percent below its 2019 level.
- **(d)** From year to year, velocity was far from constant: people and firms first held on to the new money, and
  spent it later. Over the six years as a whole, velocity changed little, so M2 and nominal GDP grew by similar
  amounts, and much of the extra nominal GDP was higher prices. That fits the quantity theory as a theory of the long
  run; it does not tell us when the money would be spent.

</details>

**Problem 7 (Challenge): Two ways to average inflation.** Fig. 4 reports Venezuela's average inflation over
1990–2025 as 2,614 percent a year. That is the arithmetic mean of its yearly inflation rates. The Model overview uses
another average: the constant rate that links the first and the last price level, $\bar{\pi} = (P_T/P_0)^{1/T} - 1$,
called the **compound** average here.

(a) With `inflation_panel.csv`, reproduce the arithmetic average for Venezuela over 1990–2025, and compute its compound
average. By what factor did Venezuela's prices rise over these years?

(b) Compute both averages for every economy over 1990–2025. List the five economies with the highest arithmetic
average next to their compound average. Which of the five falls furthest when the economies are ranked by the compound
average?

(c) Prove that, for two years, the arithmetic average of the gross rates $1+\pi_1$ and $1+\pi_2$ is never smaller than
the compound average, and that the two are equal only when $\pi_1 = \pi_2$.

(d) Which average should a test of the quantity theory use? Use the log form of equation (3).

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

$P_T/P_0$ is the product of the gross rates $1 + \pi_t/100$; pandas has `.prod()` for it. For (c), compare the squares
of the two averages: expand $\left(1 + \frac{\pi_1 + \pi_2}{2}\right)^2 - (1 + \pi_1)(1 + \pi_2)$ and simplify.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a) and (b).** Add a column with the gross rates, then compute both averages for Venezuela and for every economy:

```python
inflation_rows = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "inflation_panel.csv")
since_1990 = inflation_rows[inflation_rows.year >= 1990].copy()
since_1990["gross"] = 1 + since_1990.inflation / 100
venezuela = since_1990[since_1990.country == "Venezuela"]
price_factor = venezuela.gross.prod()
print(f"Venezuela {venezuela.year.min()}-{venezuela.year.max()} ({len(venezuela)} years): "
      f"arithmetic {venezuela.inflation.mean():,.1f}%, compound {100 * (price_factor ** (1 / len(venezuela)) - 1):.1f}%, "
      f"prices x {price_factor:.2g}")
by_country = since_1990.groupby("country")
averages_1990 = pd.DataFrame({"arithmetic": by_country.inflation.mean(),
                              "compound": 100 * (by_country.gross.prod() ** (1 / by_country.gross.count()) - 1)})
averages_1990["compound rank"] = averages_1990.compound.rank(ascending=False)
print(averages_1990.sort_values("arithmetic", ascending=False).head(5).round(1))
```

Our data for Venezuela end in 2024 (35 years). The arithmetic average is 2,614.0 percent, as in Fig. 4, but the
compound average is only 147.4 percent a year. Prices rose by a factor of about $6 \times 10^{13}$. The five highest
arithmetic averages are Venezuela (2,614.0; compound 147.4), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (995.4; 124.7),
Georgia (587.7; 49.4), Angola (311.0; 99.0) and Brazil (238.7; 55.5 percent). Georgia falls furthest, from third to
eighth place: its arithmetic average is dominated by three hyperinflation years, 1992–1994 (15,607 percent in 1994). A single year of
65,374 percent, like Venezuela's 2018, adds 1,868 points to a 35-year arithmetic mean, but its gross rate of 655 enters
the compound average only through its 35th root.

**(c)** Let $a = \pi_1$ and $b = \pi_2$. The squared arithmetic average of the gross rates, minus their product, is

$$\left(1 + \frac{a+b}{2}\right)^2 - (1+a)(1+b) = 1 + (a+b) + \frac{(a+b)^2}{4} - 1 - a - b - ab = \frac{(a+b)^2 - 4ab}{4} = \frac{(a-b)^2}{4} \ge 0.$$

So $\left(1 + \frac{a+b}{2}\right)^2 \ge (1+a)(1+b)$, and taking square roots, $1 + \frac{a+b}{2} \ge \sqrt{(1+a)(1+b)}$:
the arithmetic average is at least the compound average, with equality only when $a = b$. (The same holds for any
number of years: it is the inequality between the arithmetic and the geometric mean.) The more inflation varies, the
bigger the gap.

**(d)** Taking logs of equation (3) in two years and subtracting gives, exactly,
$\Delta\ln M + \Delta\ln V = \Delta\ln P + \Delta\ln Y$. Averaging over the years keeps the identity exact, and the
average of $\Delta \ln P = \ln(1+\pi_t)$ is the log of one plus the compound average. So a test of the quantity theory
should compare compound (or log) averages of money growth and inflation. Arithmetic averages give crisis years far too
much weight: they push the high-inflation economies of Fig. 4 up and to the right, and by different amounts for money
and prices when the two series cover different years.

</details>

### Modeling problems

**Problem 8 (Basic): India's inflation target.** Since 2016, the Reserve Bank of India has had to keep CPI inflation
at 4 percent, within a band of 2 to 6 percent ([Reserve Bank of India 2025](https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/PublicationsView.aspx?id=23171)).
The IMF projects India's real GDP to grow by about 7 percent a year in 2026–2031
([IMF, World Economic Outlook](https://www.imf.org/external/datamapper/NGDP_RPCH@WEO/IND)). Use the calculator below,
which is built on equations (5) and (6).

(a) Suppose the RBI followed a fixed rule instead: broad money grows by 11 percent a year, the 4 percent target plus
the IMF's 7 percent, as if velocity never changed. With real GDP growing by 7 percent, which range of velocity growth
keeps inflation inside the 2–6 percent band? Find the edges with the velocity slider, then check them with equation (5).

(b) In the data of Fig. 4, India's broad money grew by 15.2 percent a year over 1990–2021 and inflation averaged 7.2
percent, while real GDP grew by 6.0 percent a year ([IMF](https://www.imf.org/external/datamapper/NGDP_RPCH@WEO/IND)).
Use equation (5) to find the growth rate of velocity that these numbers imply.

(c) Is the velocity growth of (b) inside your range from (a)? If velocity kept falling at that rate, where in the band
would the 11 percent rule leave inflation, and how much room would be left for a year in which velocity falls faster?
What does this say about a money-growth rule that assumes constant velocity?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Equation (5) can be solved for any one of its four growth rates. In the calculator, keep money growth at 11 and real
GDP growth at 7, and move velocity growth until the title says that the dot has left the band. With money growth and
real GDP growth fixed, each point of velocity growth moves inflation by one point.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
def target_calculator(g_M=11.0, g_Y=7.0, g_V=0.0):
    """Practice: inflation from equation (5), pi = g_M + g_V - g_Y, against a 4% target with a 2-6% band."""
    money = np.linspace(0, 25, 101)
    pi = qt_inflation(g_M, g_Y, g_V)
    exact = 100 * ((1 + g_M / 100) * (1 + g_V / 100) / (1 + g_Y / 100) - 1)
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_hrect(y0=2, y1=6, fillcolor=GREEN, opacity=0.15, line_width=0,
                  annotation_text="target 4%, band 2–6%", annotation_position="top left")
    fig.add_hline(y=4, line_dash="dash", line_color=GREEN)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=money, y=qt_inflation(money, g_Y, g_V), mode="lines", name="π = g_M + g_V − g_Y",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[g_M], y=[pi], mode="markers", name="your money growth", marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=12)))
    where = "inside" if 2 <= pi <= 6 else "outside"
    fig.update_layout(title=f"g_M = {g_M:.1f}%: inflation {round(pi, 1) + 0.0:.1f}% (exact {round(exact, 1) + 0.0:.1f}%), "
                            f"{where} the 2–6% band",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Money growth g_M (percent a year)", range=[0, 25]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Inflation π (percent)", range=[-10, 20], tickvals=[-5, 0, 5, 10, 15]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.02, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom"))
    return fig


interact(target_calculator,
         g_M=FloatSlider(value=11, min=5, max=20, step=0.5, description="money growth g_M (percent)", style=WIDE),
         g_Y=FloatSlider(value=7, min=4, max=9, step=0.5, description="real GDP growth g_Y (percent)", style=WIDE),
         g_V=FloatSlider(value=0, min=-3, max=3, step=0.5, description="velocity growth g_V (percent)", style=WIDE));
```

**Source.** A calculator built on the quantity theory of the Model overview, equations (5) and (6), adapted from the
discussion in Chapter 8 of Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Under the rule, equation (5) gives $\pi = \bar{g}_M + \bar{g}_V - \bar{g}_Y = 11 + \bar{g}_V - 7 = 4 + \bar{g}_V$.
Inflation stays in the band while $2 \le 4 + \bar{g}_V \le 6$, that is, for velocity growth between $-2$ and $+2$ percent
a year. The calculator agrees: the title says "inside" from $\bar{g}_V = -2$ to $+2$, and "outside" at $-2.5$ and $+2.5$.
The range is 4 points wide, as wide as the band, because each point of velocity growth moves inflation by one point.
With the exact formula in the title, $1.11\,(1 + \bar{g}_V)/1.07 - 1$, the range runs from about $-1.7$ to $+2.2$ percent.

**(b)** Solve equation (5) for velocity growth: $\bar{g}_V = \pi + \bar{g}_Y - \bar{g}_M = 7.2 + 6.0 - 15.2 = -2.0$
percent a year. India's velocity of broad money fell by about 2 percent a year: money grew faster than nominal GDP, for
example because more people kept their savings in bank deposits, which count as broad money.

**(c)** The $-2.0$ percent of (b) sits right on the lower edge of the range from (a). If velocity kept falling at
that rate, the 11 percent rule would give inflation of $11 - 2 - 7 = 2$ percent, the bottom of the band, and the exact
formula gives 1.7 percent, just below it. No room is left: any year in which velocity falls faster than 2 percent
pushes inflation out of the band. Check the edges with the model function:

```python
for velocity in (-2.5, -2.0, 0.0, 2.0, 2.5):
    shortcut_pi = qt_inflation(11, 7, g_V=velocity)                      # equation (5)
    exact_pi = 100 * (1.11 * (1 + velocity / 100) / 1.07 - 1)
    print(f"g_V = {velocity:+.1f}%: inflation {shortcut_pi:.1f}% (exact {exact_pi:.1f}%), "
          f"inside the band: {2 <= shortcut_pi <= 6}")
```

A rule that assumes constant velocity would have kept India at the very edge of the band. A money-growth rule works only
if the central bank knows velocity growth, and a mistake of 2 points in velocity is a mistake of 2 points in inflation.
That is one reason why inflation-targeting central banks aim at inflation itself, rather than at a fixed growth rate of
money.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 9 (Intermediate): Should the tax on interest ignore inflation?** In a hypothetical country, inflation is
steady and everyone expects it, so the nominal interest rate follows the Fisher equation (7), $i = R + \pi$, with a
real rate of $R = 2$ percent. Interest income is taxed at 30 percent of its nominal amount. The finance ministry
considers taxing only the real part of interest, $i - \pi$ (an **indexed** tax). The calculator below draws the
saver's after-tax real return under both rules.

(a) Read off the after-tax real return and the effective tax rate under the current rule, at 2 percent and at 8 percent
inflation.

(b) Derive the inflation rate at which the after-tax real return under the current rule turns negative, and check it
with the sliders.

(c) How much does indexing raise the after-tax real return at 8 percent inflation? How much tax does the government
then give up per 100 dollars of savings each year?

(d) Why might a government that runs high inflation prefer not to index? Link your answer to the fiscal causes of high
inflation.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

The Model overview shows that the after-tax real return under the current rule is $(1-\tau)R - \tau\pi$; set it to
zero for (b). The tax per 100 dollars is $\tau i$ dollars under the current rule and $\tau(i - \pi)$ dollars with
indexing.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
def saver_calculator(pi=8.0, tau=0.3, R=2.0):
    """Practice: after-tax real return (1 - tau) i - pi with i = R + pi (equation (7)), and with an indexed tax."""
    inflation = np.linspace(0, 16, 65)
    after = (1 - tau) * nominal_rate(R, pi) - pi                     # tax on nominal interest
    indexed = (1 - tau) * R                                          # tax on real interest only
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=inflation, y=(1 - tau) * nominal_rate(R, inflation) - inflation, mode="lines",
                             name="tax on nominal interest", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, 16], y=[indexed, indexed], mode="lines", name="tax on real interest (indexed)",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[pi, pi], y=[after, indexed], mode="markers", name="at this inflation rate",
                             marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=11)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"π = {pi:.1f}%: after-tax real return {round(after, 2) + 0.0:.2f}% (indexed {indexed:.2f}%), "
                            f"effective tax {100 * (R - after) / R:.0f}%",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Inflation π (percent)", range=[0, 16]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="After-tax real return (percent)", range=[-8, 5], tickvals=[-6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4]),
                      legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.15, yanchor="top"))
    return fig


interact(saver_calculator,
         pi=FloatSlider(value=8, min=0.5, max=15, step=0.5, description="inflation π (percent)", style=WIDE),
         tau=FloatSlider(value=0.3, min=0.1, max=0.5, step=0.05, description="tax rate τ (share)", style=WIDE),
         R=FloatSlider(value=2, min=1, max=4, step=0.5, description="real rate R (percent)", style=WIDE));
```

in the Model overview, adapted from the discussion in Chapter 8 of Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** With $\tau = 0.3$ and $R = 2$, the after-tax real return is $(1-\tau)R - \tau\pi = 1.4 - 0.3\pi$. At 2 percent
inflation it is $1.4 - 0.6 = 0.80$ percent, and the effective tax rate, $\tau(1 + \pi/R)$, is $0.3 \times 2 = 60$
percent. At 8 percent inflation it is $1.4 - 2.4 = -1.00$ percent, and the effective tax rate is
$0.3 \times 5 = 150$ percent: the tax takes more than the whole real return.

**(b)** Set the return to zero and solve for $\pi$:

$$(1-\tau)R - \tau\pi = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \pi = \frac{(1-\tau)R}{\tau} = \frac{0.7 \times 2}{0.3} = 4.67 \text{ percent}.$$

With the sliders, the blue line crosses zero between 4.5 percent (a return of +0.05 percent) and 5 percent (−0.10
percent). The higher the tax rate or the lower the real rate, the lower this threshold.

**(c)** With indexing the after-tax real return is $(1-\tau)R = 1.40$ percent at any inflation rate, so at 8 percent
inflation it rises by $1.40 - (-1.00) = 2.40$ points, which is exactly $\tau\pi$. Per 100 dollars of savings, the
nominal interest is 10 dollars: the current rule takes $0.3 \times 10 = 3.00$ dollars of tax, the indexed rule
$0.3 \times 2 = 0.60$ dollars. The government gives up 2.40 dollars per 100 dollars a year.

```python
tax_share, real_r = 0.3, 2
for infl in (2, 8):
    i_nominal = nominal_rate(real_r, infl)
    print(f"pi = {infl}%: after-tax real return {(1 - tax_share) * i_nominal - infl:+.2f}%, "
          f"tax per 100 dollars {tax_share * i_nominal:.2f} (indexed {tax_share * (i_nominal - infl):.2f})")
```

It prints an after-tax real return of +0.80 percent and a tax of 1.20 dollars (0.60 indexed) at 2 percent inflation,
and −1.00 percent and 3.00 dollars (0.60 indexed) at 8 percent.

**(d)** Under the current rule, the tax on saving rises with inflation without any vote on a new tax: at 8 percent the
government collects five times as much from each saver as with indexing. A government short of revenue gains from
inflation twice, through the inflation tax on money (equation (10)) and through taxes written in nominal terms. That
gives it a reason not to index, and one more reason to let inflation run, which is the fiscal side of high inflation.

</details>

**Problem 10 (Challenge): How much can the printing press raise?** A hypothetical government has lost access to loans
and must pay a deficit of 3 percent of GDP with new money. The velocity of its currency is 12, and real GDP grows by 3
percent a year.

(a) With constant velocity, use the calculator to find the money growth and the inflation rate that pay for the
deficit. Check them with step 4 of the seigniorage block in the Model overview.

(b) People hold less currency when it loses value fast, so velocity rises with money growth. Suppose that
$V = \bar{V}(1+\bar{g}_M)^a$ with $a > 0$. Show that seigniorage is then $\bar{g}_M/[\bar{V}(1+\bar{g}_M)^{1+a}]$ of
GDP, and that it is largest at $\bar{g}_M = 1/a$. How much can the press raise at most when $a = 1$?

(c) With $a = 1$, can the government still pay its deficit of 3 percent of GDP? What about a deficit of 1.5 percent?
Find the two money growth rates that raise 1.5 percent. Which one would you choose, and why?

(d) According to equation (9), what has to happen to end the inflation?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

For (b), start from the exact seigniorage $\bar{g}_M/[(1+\bar{g}_M)V]$ of equation (10), take logs, and set the
derivative with respect to $\bar{g}_M$ to zero. For (c), with $a = 1$ the condition "seigniorage = 1.5 percent of GDP"
is a quadratic equation in $\bar{g}_M$. In the calculator, choose the velocity response $a$ with the menu.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
def press_calculator(sigma=3.0, V=12.0, a=0.0):
    """Practice: seigniorage 100 g / [V (1 + g)^(1 + a)] (equation (10), velocity V (1 + g)^a) and a deficit sigma."""
    g = np.geomspace(0.01, 200, 400)                               # money growth: 1% to 20,000% a year
    fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=100 * g, y=100 * g / (V * (1 + g) ** (1 + a)), mode="lines",
                               name="seigniorage", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_hline(y=sigma, line_dash="dash", line_color=GREEN, annotation_text=f"deficit: {sigma:.1f}% of GDP",
                  annotation_position="top left")
    rising = np.geomspace(0.001, 200 if a == 0 else 1 / a, 2001)    # seigniorage rises up to g = 1/a
    revenue = 100 * rising / (V * (1 + rising) ** (1 + a))
    best = 100 / V if a == 0 else revenue[-1]                       # the ceiling 1/V, or the peak at g = 1/a
    if sigma <= revenue[-1]:
        needed = np.interp(sigma, revenue, rising)                  # read the rising curve backwards
        pi = 100 * ((1 + needed) / 1.03 - 1)                        # exact quantity theory, real growth 3%
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[100 * needed], y=[sigma], mode="markers", name="deficit paid",
                                 marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=12)))
        title = f"Deficit {sigma:.1f}% of GDP: money growth {100 * needed:,.0f}%, inflation {pi:,.0f}% a year"
    else:
        title = f"A deficit of {sigma:.1f}% of GDP cannot be paid: the press raises at most {best:.2f}%"
    fig.update_layout(title=title, yaxis=dict(title="Seigniorage (percent of GDP)", range=[0, 14], tickvals=[2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]),
                      xaxis=dict(type="log", title="Money growth g_M (percent a year, ratio scale)",
                                 range=[0, np.log10(20000)], tickvals=[1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000]))
    return fig


interact(press_calculator, sigma=FloatSlider(value=3, min=0.5, max=8, step=0.5, description="deficit (percent of GDP)", style=WIDE),
         V=FloatSlider(value=12, min=8, max=20, step=2, description="velocity of currency V", style=WIDE),
         a=Dropdown(options=[0, 0.5, 1, 2], value=0, description="velocity response a", style=WIDE));
```

**Source.** A calculator built on the government budget constraint and equation (10) of the Model overview (the
velocity response $a$ is our own extension), adapted from the discussion of the inflation tax in Chapter 8 of
Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** With $\sigma = 0.03$ and $\bar{V} = 12$, $\sigma\bar{V} = 0.36$, so step 4 gives
$\bar{g}_M = \sigma\bar{V}/(1 - \sigma\bar{V}) = 0.36/0.64 = 56.25$ percent, and the exact quantity theory gives
inflation of $1.5625/1.03 - 1 = 51.7$ percent a year. The calculator's title shows 56 and 52 percent.

**(b)** By equation (10), seigniorage is $\bar{g}_M/[(1+\bar{g}_M)V]$. Put in $V = \bar{V}(1+\bar{g}_M)^a$:

$$s(\bar{g}_M) = \frac{\bar{g}_M}{(1+\bar{g}_M)\,\bar{V}(1+\bar{g}_M)^a} = \frac{\bar{g}_M}{\bar{V}(1+\bar{g}_M)^{1+a}}.$$

Take logs, $\ln s = \ln\bar{g}_M - (1+a)\ln(1+\bar{g}_M) - \ln\bar{V}$, and set the derivative to zero:

$$\frac{1}{\bar{g}_M} - \frac{1+a}{1+\bar{g}_M} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 1 + \bar{g}_M = (1+a)\,\bar{g}_M \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar{g}_M = \frac{1}{a}.$$

Over a common denominator the derivative is $(1 - a\bar{g}_M)/[\bar{g}_M(1+\bar{g}_M)]$: positive below $1/a$ and
negative above it, so this is the maximum. Putting $\bar{g}_M = 1/a$ back
in gives $s_{\max} = a^a/[\bar{V}(1+a)^{1+a}]$. With $a = 1$ the peak is at 100 percent money growth, and
$s_{\max} = 1/(4\bar{V}) = 1/48 = 2.08$ percent of GDP, a quarter of the constant-velocity ceiling of 8.33 percent.

**(c)** No: 3 percent is more than the 2.08 percent the press can raise, and the calculator says so. Printing faster
than 100 percent a year only lowers the revenue, because people hold so much less money. A government that tries
anyway gets ever faster money growth and inflation: a hyperinflation. A deficit of 1.5 percent can be paid. With
$a = 1$, $\bar{V} = 12$ and $s = 0.015$, the condition $\bar{g}_M = 0.18\,(1+\bar{g}_M)^2$ becomes

$$0.18\,\bar{g}_M^2 - 0.64\,\bar{g}_M + 0.18 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar{g}_M = \frac{0.64 \pm \sqrt{0.64^2 - 4 \times 0.18^2}}{2 \times 0.18},$$

so $\bar{g}_M = 30.8$ percent or $\bar{g}_M = 324.8$ percent, with inflation of 27.0 or 312.4 percent a year. Both raise
the same revenue, so the government should choose the low one: the high one taxes money holders much harder for
nothing. The calculator marks the low one (31 percent and 27 percent in its title); the high one is where the blue
curve crosses the dashed line again on the right.

```python
for root in (1, -1):
    g_root = (0.64 - root * (0.64 ** 2 - 4 * 0.18 ** 2) ** 0.5) / (2 * 0.18)
    print(f"money growth {100 * g_root:.1f}%, inflation {100 * ((1 + g_root) / 1.03 - 1):.1f}%, "
          f"seigniorage {100 * g_root / (12 * (1 + g_root) ** 2):.2f}% of GDP")
```

**(d)** Equation (9) says $\Delta M = G - T - \Delta B$. Money growth, and with it inflation, can fall only if spending
falls, taxes rise, or the government can borrow again. A new currency or a promise from the central bank does not
change this arithmetic; a credible budget does.

</details>
